build 2026-06-25.369  (v2.10.98)

Next enhancement tier: schema caching (perf) + three stability hardenings.

PERF -- column types are CACHED per table. The sidebar tree and the field
explorer call the DESCRIBE + typeof() probe on every expand, and on a
multi-GB nested view the typeof() fallback reads a live row each time --
expensive to repeat. The answer is now cached per table and handed out as a
copy; DML can't change types, and every path that CAN (loads, DDL, drops,
rebuilds, sync_catalog) invalidates -- with a structural test asserting every
registry write in the engine drops the cache entry, so a future write site
can't forget. Field trees open instantly after the first probe.

STABILITY 1 -- reuse can never shadow a real table. A journal cell whose name
matches an existing table/view now bounces as reuse_stale (case-insensitive)
instead of standing up a TEMP view that would shadow the user's table for the
duration of the query. That closes the one documented caveat from .361; the
client silently falls back to full inlining.

STABILITY 2 -- filecache commit hardened for Windows. os.replace can
transiently fail when an AV scanner / indexer pins the target: commit now
retries briefly; a persistent pin raises and the LOAD still succeeds by
moving the finished conversion to a per-instance temp (uncached), leaving
nothing half-published in the cache dir.

STABILITY 3 -- read cursors are BOUNDED. Each concurrent read cursor is a
live DuckDB connection; spamming Run now degrades gracefully to the locked
path when the slots (SAMQL_READ_CURSORS, default 4, clamped 1..64) are
exhausted, instead of opening ever more connections. Slots release after
every run, including cancels.

In-depth tests: types-cache battery (hit/copy/per-table drop/full clear +
the every-write-invalidates structural invariant), cursor-cap battery
(exhausted -> locked with NO new connection; free -> lock-free AND the slot
provably released; env clamp), commit-hardening battery (retry past
transient pins; persistent pin raises), plus the collision case in the reuse
battery and the pinned-commit fallback case in the load wiring.

engines.py, session.py, filecache.py, run_tests.py. Suite: 548 passing, 0
failing, 21 skipped. No new dependencies.

build 2026-06-25.363  (v2.10.92)

Optimization #2: read queries run on their OWN cursor -- true concurrency.

The DuckDB read path (the result COPY) no longer serializes on the engine's
write lock: when the concurrency flag is on (default since .361), an eligible
read runs on a separate cursor -- DuckDB's documented one-cursor-per-thread
MVCC model, the same primitive the metadata reads and streaming export already
use. Two journal cells can genuinely overlap, and a long query no longer
blocks a load (or vice versa).

Four rails, each tested:
  - a run using R1 reuse views is PINNED to the locked main connection (TEMP
    views are invisible to a fresh cursor) -- correctness beats concurrency;
  - a cancel/interrupt RE-RAISES as cancelled -- never silently rerun;
  - any other cursor failure (e.g. a TEMP staging table a fresh cursor can't
    see) falls back to the locked path with a FRESH temp file, and the failed
    attempt's partial file is removed;
  - the running cursor registers itself under the query id, so cancel_query /
    the per-op X interrupts the RIGHT statement (the engine-level interrupt
    only reaches the main connection); the engine mapping is restored after.

SAMQL_CONCURRENT_READS=0 turns the whole family off (reads then serialize on
the lock exactly as before .361).

In-depth tests: a 6-scenario behavioral battery (cursor COPY with the lock
never acquired; reuse pin; flag-off back-compat; fallback + fresh temp;
interrupt propagation; live cancel-handle routing with mapping restore) plus
source guards. session.py only. Suite: 529 passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped.
No new dependencies.

build 2026-06-25.362  (v2.10.91)

Optimization #1: the file->Parquet conversion cache now SURVIVES restarts.

Loading a large JSON/CSV converts it once to Parquet and queries that in
place; that cache used to live in the per-PID temp dir, which the clean-exit
lifecycle wipes -- so every app start re-paid the full 1.7 GB parse. It now
lives in a stable <temp>/samql/filecache/ directory keyed by the source's
identity (absolute path + size + mtime + reader kind/options + a format
version), so restarting the app -- or the manifest restore after a restart --
reattaches the existing Parquet in milliseconds instead of minutes.

  - Correctness first: the key changes whenever the source changes, so a
    stale entry can NEVER be served -- it just stops being found and ages
    out. A format-version bump invalidates everything. Conversions publish
    atomically (temp name + rename), so a crash mid-COPY can't leave a half
    entry under the final name.
  - Budgeted + aged: SAMQL_FILECACHE_GB (default 10) caps the total with
    least-recently-USED eviction (hits touch the entry); SAMQL_FILECACHE_DAYS
    (default 14) drops anything unused that long. Startup runs the sweep.
    SAMQL_FILECACHE=0 disables the whole thing (old behavior).
  - The per-instance lifecycle is untouched: sweep_stale explicitly exempts
    the cache dir, and everything else still lives + dies per PID.

In-depth tests (4 new): key identity (size/mtime/kind/options/version),
hit/miss/atomic-publish/LRU-touch/kill-switch, sweep policy (abandoned temps,
age-out, LRU-to-budget, never touches foreign files), the LOAD wiring (a hit
skips the COPY entirely; a changed source misses; disabled falls back to the
per-instance temp), and lifecycle (stray-dir sweep exemption + startup sweep).
Bundle grows to 102 files (new samql_core/filecache.py).

engines.py, tmputil.py, server.py, filecache.py (new). Suite: 527 passing, 0
failing, 21 skipped. No new dependencies.

build 2026-06-25.361  (v2.10.90)

The audit's big three, fixed -- plus live engine tuning (R4).

R1 -- Journal chain reuse (F8, the one you measured). A chained cell no longer
re-executes its upstream: the Journal sends a REDUCED query plus a reuse map
{cell name -> result id}, and the server stands up TEMP VIEWs over those
cells' already-computed parquet results for the duration of the run. A fresh
"SELECT count(*) FROM cell2" now reads cell2's 214-row parquet instead of
re-scanning 1.7 GB and re-exploding the legs. Safety rails: only FRESH,
UNCAPPED DuckDB results are reused (a capped store is not the full answer);
anything evicted/ineligible bounces as reuse_stale and the client retries once
with full CTE inlining; staleness still keys off the canonical composition, so
invalidation behavior is unchanged. Group aliases reuse the same way.

R2 -- Concurrent reads default ON (F2/F12). Metadata reads (tables panel,
counts, schema) run on separate cursors by default, so they stay live while a
build/load holds the main connection. SAMQL_CONCURRENT_READS=0 restores the
old fully-serialized behavior if anything looks off.

R3 -- No more row_number() window on results (F1). The result COPY writes the
query output directly; the stable "__rn" paging/tiebreak column is synthesized
at READ time from parquet's file_row_number (1-based, so every consumer --
paging, sorting, filtering, export -- is unchanged). Big results skip a full
single-threaded sequencing pass and COPY can parallelize. The COPY is now also
keepalive-guarded like other long native statements (heartbeats, cancel
nudges) -- previously it evaded that guard.

R4 -- Settings -> "Engine tuning (memory / threads)...": adjust DuckDB's
memory_limit and thread count live for this session (non-blocking -- a busy
engine says so instead of queueing). SAMQL_DUCKDB_MEMORY_GB persists across
restarts. The audit doc's follow-ups section is updated to reflect all four
shipped.

build 2026-06-25.353  (v2.10.82)

Fix the "checking..." status (and frozen-feeling UI) during a large load.

Root cause was the memory widget, not the status endpoint. The widget polls
DuckDB memory every few seconds, and that probe ran through the locked execute()
path -- so while a big load held the engine's write lock for its whole duration,
each poll BLOCKED for the entire load. Several blocked polls then occupied every
slot in the browser's per-host connection pool, starving the (lock-free)
/api/status poll -- which left the server card stuck on "checking...".

  - the DuckDB memory probe (engines.memory_bytes) now acquires the write lock
    NON-BLOCKING: if the engine is busy it reports "unknown" instead of queuing
    behind the load, so the memory poll can never pile up and exhaust the pool.
    memory_usage() routes through it.
  - the status hook now caches its last snapshot at module scope, so the memory
    popover (which unmounts when closed) shows the last-known status immediately
    on reopen instead of flashing/sticking on "checking..." until its first poll
    returns.

engines.py + session.py (non-blocking memory probe), ActivityShared.tsx (cached
status). Note: closing a load modal aborts the client's in-flight requests but
the backend load keeps running -- that's expected; the fix stops the memory poll
from wedging the pool while it does. Suite: 513 passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped.
No new dependencies.

build 2026-06-25.352  (v2.10.81)

Fix a test that failed on Windows (PyCharm), plus harden temp cleanup.

The "a session's temp data is cleared on exit and next start" test failed on a
box where DuckDB is installed. Cause was the TEST, not the product: the running
suite holds a live DuckDB connection whose db file + spill dir live inside the
instance dir, and Windows refuses to rmtree a directory that still has open
handles -- so checking cleanup against the live dir mid-suite is invalid. (At a
real shutdown _graceful_shutdown recycles the engines first, closing those
handles, THEN removes the dir -- so exit cleanup was always correct.)

  - the test now runs against a throwaway directory with its files written
    through a closed context manager, so no handle lingers -- deterministic on
    any OS, independent of whether DuckDB is present.
  - temp cleanup (_rmtree) is now hardened for Windows read-only leftovers: a
    normal rmtree, then -- if anything survives -- clear the read-only bit on
    the leftovers and retry. Used by cleanup_instance / reset_instance /
    sweep_stale.

tmputil.py (hardened _rmtree), tests/run_tests.py (isolated test + wiring
assertion). Suite: 512 passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped. No new dependencies.

build 2026-06-25.350  (v2.10.79)

Guarantee: a new session never inherits a previous session's temp data.

Every temporary artifact SamQL writes -- the DuckDB on-disk database and its
spill dir, the SQLite disk db, Parquet result stores (incl. the capped ones),
the large-file Parquet cache, NDJSON conversions, flatten/export spill, uploads

build 2026-06-25.349  (v2.10.78)

Fix: a runaway explode no longer runs forever and wedges the whole app.

Root cause: a DuckDB read is materialized with one COPY (...) TO parquet, which
holds the engine's connection lock for its whole duration. An UNNEST cross-
product on the nested "json" column (e.g. receivingLeg x payingLeg) can produce
BILLIONS of rows, so that COPY never finishes -- the lock is held forever, every
schema/count read backs up behind it, and the browser's small connection pool
fills, so even Stop / Reset can't get through ("failed to fetch").

Now every result materialization is bounded by a safety ceiling,
SAMQL_MAX_RESULT_ROWS (default 10,000,000; set 0 to disable). The COPY gets a
LIMIT so DuckDB streams and STOPS at the ceiling -- the query finishes in
seconds instead of pinning the engine. The fallback drain path stops at the same
ceiling. When a result is capped, a notification toast says so ("Result capped
-- stopped at the N-row safety limit; add a filter or raise
SAMQL_MAX_RESULT_ROWS") -- one toast on the run, no inline clutter.

Practical guidance for the big swap file: explode receivingLeg and payingLeg in
SEPARATE cells (never cross-joined), and filter to the instruments you care
about, so you're exploding a handful of records, not all 22,704. To keep the UI
responsive during any long query, enable concurrent reads
(SAMQL_CONCURRENT_READS=1 or the in-app toggle) so schema/counts/status don't
queue behind the query's lock.

session.py (cap on both read paths + result_capped through the cache/page) and
the run handlers (toast). Suite: 509 passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped. No new
dependencies.

build 2026-06-25.341  (v2.10.70)

Selective flattening: choose which fields to flatten and load.

The decisive lever for a huge nested file. The flattener now accepts an
`exclude` list of keys/paths; a matched key is skipped entirely -- no column,
and if it is a nested array, none of the child table(s) it would have produced.
Because a skipped array's rows are never emitted, dropping the heavy arrays in a
swap-style file collapses the row count (and the write time) rather than merely
speeding it up. On the 1.7 GB sample, skipping the swap flow arrays takes the
load from ~5.9M rows / ~68 min toward the ~50k roots+links -- seconds, not an
hour.

Matching: a bare token (e.g. "cashFlows") skips that key wherever it appears; a
dotted token (e.g. "payingLeg.swapStream") skips that branch by prefix. Enter a
comma-separated list.

Wired end to end: JSONFlattener.exclude -> load_json -> load_file ->
Session.load_file -> the load endpoints (upload sync + background, and
load-by-path). The UI adds a "Skip these fields (JSON, optional)" input in both
the file-browser load panel and the drag-and-drop prompt, shown only for JSON.
Non-JSON loads are unaffected; leaving it blank flattens everything as before.
Suite: 500 passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped. No new dependencies.

build 2026-06-25.340  (v2.10.69)

Speed up the wide-table write.

The flattened-table writer coerced every value one cell at a time -- a Python
function call per cell, O(rows x cols). On a narrow table (4 cols) that is
cheap; on an 84-column swap root it is ~20x the calls per row, which is most of
why wide tables wrote ~30x slower per row than narrow ones. The coercion was
also redundant for the numeric columns (it returned them unchanged) yet ran on
every one.

The Arrow write path now prepares columns columnarly: it transposes the batch
once (a single C-level zip) and stringifies ONLY the text columns, leaving
numeric/boolean/None columns to pass straight through to Arrow with no per-cell
Python work. Per-cell coercion is confined to the executemany fallback, which
only runs if the Arrow insert fails. Behaviour is unchanged -- text columns
still land as strings, numeric columns still infer -- and the new _columnarize
helper is pure, so it is unit-tested directly (numeric/None pass through, only
text is stringified, empty batch handled).

Note on the projection: the "~1,520 rows/s" figure that drove the ~65 min write
estimate was measured on a 190-row table, so it is dominated by fixed
per-insert overhead; the real bulk write of millions of rows in large batches
amortizes that and should beat it. Suite: 499 passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped.
No new dependencies.

build 2026-06-25.339  (v2.10.68)

Guard the full analysis against an unrepresentative (capped) scan.

If the scan is capped to a handful of records on a large file (e.g. "Scan up to
N records = 10" on the 1.7 GB file, a workaround for the earlier timeout), it
only sees the small records at the front -- so the biggest-array, projected-row,
and bottleneck numbers describe those few records, not the file. The tool used
to still print a confident verdict ("write-width", "2.1s") off that tiny sample.

Now, when the scan stops at a small cap on a substantial file (hit the cap, fewer
than 5000 records seen, file over 20 MB), the analysis reports bottleneck
"scan-too-small", suppresses the (meaningless) full-load projection, and tells
you to set "Scan up to N records" to 0 to scan the whole file -- which is safe
now because the scan is time-boxed (build .338) and will not hang. The byte
fraction is deliberately NOT used for this decision (the reader buffers ahead,
so it overstates coverage on a tiny scan). Suite: 499 passing, 0 failing, 21
skipped. No new dependencies.

itself into the finding.

The whole-file scan reading the real 1.7 GB file took longer than the request
allows. That is itself a result (reading the file is not fast), but the tool has
to survive it. Now the scan runs under a wall-clock budget (default 45s,
adjustable) and:

  - tracks the REAL byte position, so it reports how far it got (MB covered) and
    the actual read throughput (MB/s);
  - if it doesn't finish, EXTRAPOLATES the full read time from that rate and
    labels the projection as extrapolated -- e.g. "covered 260 MB of 1749 MB
    (~5.8 MB/s), full read alone ~5 min";
  - aborts even if it gets stuck parsing one enormous record: the reader is given
    a budget-based cancel, so a single huge record can't run past the budget;
  - skips flattening the heaviest record when it projects to > 500k rows (it's
    reported from the scan instead), so that step can't blow the budget either.

New verdict "read-throughput" fires when the file simply can't be read fast
enough in the budget -- the read, before any write, is the cost (big/deeply
nested records make ijson slow; SAMQL_JSON_READER=stdlib helps). The projection
now splits into read + write, and the diagnostic request timeout was raised to 5
minutes. Adjustable "Scan time budget (seconds)" param added. Suite: 499
passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped. No new dependencies.



One comprehensive diagnostic: "Full load analysis (start here)".

No more running piecemeal checks and reporting back. This single diagnostic runs
every analysis in one pass and ends with a named bottleneck and a projected
full-load time. It is now the default selection in Settings -> Diagnostics (and
`python tools/diag_load.py <file> --full` on the CLI).

In one run it does:
  1. Environment + features.
  2. A WHOLE-FILE read-only structural scan: record count, byte size, read
     throughput, the heaviest records, the biggest nested array + max depth, and
     the TOTAL projected row count (sum of all nested array lengths) -- so it
     sees the whole file and the total volume without flattening anything.
  3. A reader comparison (ijson vs stdlib) on a sample.
  4. A flatten of the front sample -> flatten throughput + the resulting table
     shape (how many tables, how wide).
  5. A write of every one of those tables to a scratch engine: per-table timing
     and throughput, cold-vs-warm, and any per-table write ERROR (a write error
     is what makes the real load fall back to the slow nested path).
  6. A flatten of the SINGLE heaviest record it just found (auto-offset) -- so a
     record that explodes is measured directly, not guessed.
  7. A projection of the full-load time from the measured throughputs, and a
     VERDICT that names which outcome it is: single-record-explosion,
     row-volume, write-width, write-error-fallback, reader-ijson, read-error, or
     none.

The result view leads with the verdict and the projected time, then shows every
phase. Bounded: only a small sample and the one heaviest record are actually
flattened/written; the whole-file part is read-only and stays fast even when a
record is a bomb. Suite: 499 passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped. No new dependencies.



New diagnostic: find the record that explodes the flatten.

The profiler keeps saying the front of the file is fast because that's all it
samples -- but a deep-flatten load can still crawl if a single record deep in
the file has a giant nested array: flattening it emits that many child rows in
one add_record, so the load stalls while the byte position sits still (and, as
seen, the cancel was slow because it was stuck in that read/flatten step). The
per-table numbers also show width costs a lot on the write (a 58-column table
wrote ~50x slower per row than a 4-column one), so a very wide OR very tall
table from a swap record is the thing to look for.

Added "JSON heaviest records (find the explosion)": it scans the WHOLE file
reading only (no flatten, so it stays fast even when a record is a bomb) and
reports the records with the biggest nested array and highest element count. If
one record has a multi-million-element array, that is the crawl, named exactly
(record index + array size) instead of guessed. It flags the file "explosive"
when the biggest array crosses 100k.

The diagnostic registry is dynamic, so this appears in Settings -> Diagnostics
automatically with its own result view. Suite: 498 passing, 0 failing, 21
skipped. No new dependencies.



Fix the slow cancel on a JSON flatten load.

The deep-flatten read loop pulled records with no cancel hook, so a Stop was
only noticed at the flattener's every-5000-row progress checkpoint. While the
reader was grinding through the file (or one big record), a cancel could hang
for a long time -- exactly what you hit. (Notably, a slow cancel is itself a
tell that the load was in the flatten path, not the nested-Parquet fallback: the
fallback already polls the cancel flag per record and interrupts its DuckDB
statement, so it stops promptly.)

  - load_json now gives the reader a cancel predicate, so a Stop is observed on
    every raw chunk -- it lands inside the read, even mid-record, instead of
    waiting for the next 5000-row checkpoint. The predicate OR's two signals: a
    hook attached to the load's progress callback (works on every engine) and
    the engine's own _cancel event (set by interrupt_loads on a Stop).
  - The engine cancel event is cleared at the start of each load, so a stale
    cancel left by a previous, already-unwound load can't spuriously abort a
    fresh one.
  - A read cancel raises an interrupt that _is_interrupt already recognizes, so
    it unwinds as a clean cancellation and does NOT trip the slow nested
    fallback.

Both new streaming load entry points (drag/drop and load-by-path) attach the
predicate. Suite: 497 passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped. No new dependencies.



Make the profiler run the REAL write path, and make the slow fallback loud.

You were right that the earlier all-clear was hollow: the profiler measured the
flatten in isolation and only wrote the largest-BY-ROW-COUNT table (here a
4-column links table) to a throwaway engine. It never wrote the wide root table,
never wrote the deep swap tables, and -- critically -- never hit the case where
a table's write THROWS, which is exactly what makes the real load quietly fall
back to the slow single-table read_json path. So "every phase is fast" was true
of the wrong code.

Two changes to find the actual problem:

  1. The JSON load profiler now writes EVERY table the flatten produces, times
     each one, reports per-table throughput, and CATCHES per-table write errors
     (a red "WRITE FAILED: ..." is the smoking gun -- that error is the fallback
     trigger). It also gains an "offset" so you can skip the small instrument
     records at the front of the file and point it straight at the big swap
     records deeper in (the earlier runs only ever sampled the front).

  2. The deep-flatten -> nested-read_json fallback in load_file is no longer
     silent. When the flatten is abandoned it writes the failing exception (with
     traceback) to stderr and tags the load result with the reason
     (fallback_from_flatten), so a load that drops onto the slow path announces
     itself instead of just "mysteriously" crawling.

How to use it on your file: run the profiler with, say, offset 20000 and 40
records to reach the swaps, and watch the per-table list for a WRITE FAILED or a
slow table. If one shows up, that names the bug; if they all write fast, the
crawl is in the nested-Parquet fallback's read pass and I'll target that next.
Suite: 496 passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped. No new dependencies.



Fix a false alarm in the load profiler's write verdict.

The .332 verdict compared the cold write against the warm write, but timed the
warm write while cProfile was instrumenting it -- so the "warm" number was
inflated by profiler overhead and could come out slower than the cold one. Once
the first engine had warmed DuckDB process-wide there was no cold-start left to
see, and the binary "cold-start or slow" verdict fell through to the wrong
branch, printing a red "the write is slow even warm" on writes that were in fact
fast (e.g. 760 rows in 0.047s ~ 16k rows/sec).

  - The warm write is now timed CLEAN (no profiler); a separate third write is
    run under cProfile only to capture where any time goes (its inflated timing
    is discarded).
  - The verdict now keys on ABSOLUTE warm throughput, not the cold/warm delta,
    and reports rows/sec: it says "fast, no write bottleneck" when the engine
    clears rows quickly (still noting if a one-time cold-start was visible), and
    only flags "genuinely slow" when warm throughput is actually low -- in which
    case the profile below it names the cost.

Conclusion from your box stands and is now stated correctly: read + flatten and
the DuckDB write are both fast at steady state; there is no bottleneck left. The
original crawl was the quadratic reader fixed in .327. Suite: 495 passing, 0
failing, 21 skipped. No new dependencies.



The JSON load profiler now separates engine cold-start from the real write cost.

Running it on the real 1.7 GB file was decisive: read + flatten of 40 records is
0.052s (fast -- the quadratic-reader fix in .327 was the original crawl), while
the single DuckDB write of 160 rows took 4.75s. But a fixed multi-second cost on
160 rows (one INSERT, not per-row) looks like engine cold-start -- which the
diagnostic pays by spinning up a throwaway engine, and which the real load never
pays because it reuses the already-warm session engine.

So the profiler now writes the largest table TWICE on the same engine and
reports both, plus a cProfile of the second (warm) write:

  - C) <engine> write (cold)  -- first write; may include one-time startup
  - C) <engine> write (warm)  -- second write; the true per-load cost
  - a plain-language verdict: if warm << cold it says the cold cost was startup
    (and your live load avoids it); if warm is still slow it points you at the
    cProfile, which now names the exact function eating the time.

No behaviour change to loading itself -- this sharpens the measurement so the
next run says definitively whether the DuckDB write is a real bottleneck or a
cold-start artifact. Suite: 495 passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped. No new deps.



Diagnostics in the UI -- Settings -> Diagnostics -- built to grow.

The load profiler is no longer a script you run in a terminal; it is a modal in

  - New backend module samql_core/diagnostics.py is a registry: a diagnostic is

  - The CLI tools/diag_load.py is now a thin wrapper over that shared core, so

  - New endpoints: GET /api/diagnostics (list + a ready environment report) and

  - New UI: Settings -> Maintenance -> Diagnostics... opens a modal with the

Measure the real bottleneck on your box -- plus a reader lever.

Honest correction: the sandbox these builds are developed in has NEITHER ijson

  - C) the DuckDB write of the largest table (the writer the app uses); and
  - a cProfile of read+flatten so the single hottest function is visible.

build 2026-06-25.328  (v2.10.57)

Concatenated arrays AND objects, any mix, all on the fast reader.

Follow-up to the quadratic-reader fix. A stream of concatenated top-level values
comes in two shapes depending on the first character, and only one of them was
getting the new fast path:

  - Starts with '[' (arrays first, possibly with objects between): already
    handled by the array-aware streaming reader -- arrays unwrapped element by
    element, bare objects yielded whole, all with the index + growing-read
    decode. Unchanged.
  - Starts with '{' (objects first) with a top-level array somewhere in the
    stream: this took the fallback reader, which decoded each top-level value
    WHOLE. Concatenated objects were fine, but an embedded top-level array was
    buffered entirely in memory and yielded as one list rather than streamed
    element by element.

The fallback path is now unified on the same array-aware reader, so an embedded
array in an object-first stream is unwrapped and streamed (bounded memory) and
gets the fast decode too. The output is identical -- the flattener already
iterates a whole-array record the same way -- so nothing downstream changes;
only memory (bounded, not the whole array at once) and the decode path (fast).

One behaviour preserved on purpose: a reply that is not JSON at all (an HTML
login page whose body starts with '<', say) still raises so the REST loader can
report "the endpoint did not return JSON (HTTP ... , text/html): <snippet>"
instead of a silent zero-record load. A stream that yields valid records and
then hits a truncated tail still stops gracefully and loads what it got.

Verified here on synthetic mixed files: an array-first stream and an
object-first-with-embedded-array stream both read every record via the fast
reader with zero whole-array buffers; concatenated objects, NDJSON, single
object/array, NaN/Infinity, BOM, empty and whitespace-only bodies, non-JSON
(raises), and truncated-after-valid (graceful) all behave. Every existing reader
test passes and the concatenated-stream test now also asserts the object-first
embedded-array case is unwrapped element by element.

No new dependencies.

build 2026-06-25.327  (v2.10.56)

The actual reason flatten-on-load crawled: a quadratic JSON reader. Fixed.

Every previous round tuned the wrong thing (a faster writer, a native flatten,
Arrow inserts) because the real cost was upstream, in the streaming JSON reader
that feeds the flattener. It decoded one value at a time by re-running the
parser from the START of a growing text buffer and copying the tail after every
value (buf = buf[end:]). Both are O(n-squared) in the size of an INDIVIDUAL
record: small records were fine, but a file of large records -- the Sophis
wrappers are ~1.7 MB each -- spent almost all its time re-scanning bytes it had
already parsed. Measured here on synthetic files, read throughput collapsed as
records grew:

    record size     old reader     new reader
    77 KB           47 MB/s        69 MB/s
    1.5 MB          7.8 MB/s       59 MB/s
    4 MB            3.1 MB/s       44 MB/s

That collapse is why a multi-GB file of fat records read at kilobytes a second.

The fix: both stdlib readers now decode by advancing an INDEX into the buffer
(raw_decode at a position -- never re-slicing off the front), and when one value
runs past the end of the buffer they read a GROWING chunk (1 MB, doubling up to
16 MB) to complete it instead of nibbling 64 KB at a time and re-scanning. Read
throughput is now flat regardless of record size, and it stays fully streaming
(bounded memory) and cancellable. Every existing reader test -- concatenated
arrays/objects, NDJSON, mixed streams, NaN/Infinity, BOM, cancel-mid-read,
deep-array linkage, stream+spill equivalence -- still passes unchanged, and a new
regression test reads multi-MB concatenated records back intact and guards the
index + growing-read approach so the quadratic pattern can't return.

With the reader linear, the remaining load cost is the flattener's per-record
dict-walking (genuinely linear work) plus the Arrow bulk write from .326. On the
synthetic 1.5 MB-record file the whole read+flatten now runs at ~16 MB/s (was
~5), so the phase that was taking most of an hour on the real file should be a
few minutes. If it is still slower than you want, that is now the flatten CPU
cost, not a bug -- tell me and I will profile that next.

No behaviour change beyond speed; no new dependencies.

build 2026-06-25.326  (v2.10.55)

Deep flatten on load, accelerated -- and multi-select table delete.

The previous round flattened on load in-engine with a single SQL UNNEST. That
was SHALLOW by construction: it explodes exactly one array level, so a deeply
nested record (cashFlows -> legs -> underlyer -> basket, swapStream -> flow
lists, and so on) came out as two tables with everything below the first level
still nested. What you want -- and what the SQLite path already produced -- is
the FULL normalized tree: a child table for every nested array at every depth,
each keyed back to its parent. So the SQL UNNEST is retired from the flatten
path and the deep recursive flattener is restored as the active engine, wired to
the same "flatten on load" toggle (it runs on load / drag-and-drop; no right-
click needed). It now builds the same many-level tree you saw under SQLite,
regardless of engine.

To keep that from crawling, the load path is accelerated:

  - The DuckDB writer bulk-inserts each batch of rows through Arrow (pyarrow) --
    one columnar append instead of a row-at-a-time bind -- which is the big win
    when a deep flatten explodes into millions of child rows. Each batch is
    independent, so if an Arrow build/cast ever fails it falls back to the
    row-wise insert for just that batch: never slower than before, usually much
    faster. (Load to DuckDB, not SQLite, to get this path; SQLite has no columnar
    ingest.)
  - JSON record parsing already uses orjson when present.
  - The flattener's in-memory row buffer before it spills to disk is now RAM-
    aware: on a box with >=16 GB it buffers more before spilling (fewer, larger
    disk writes). Override with the SAMQL_JSON_SPILL_ROWS environment variable.

Honest note: this data genuinely explodes into a lot of rows, so expect the load
to take minutes, not seconds -- but the deep tree is correct and the writer is
no longer the bottleneck. If you just need it fast and can live with nested
columns, turn "flatten on load" off (a single nested read_json table lands in a
couple of minutes); or load to SQLite for the deep tree without the Arrow path.

Also new: select multiple loaded tables and drop them in one action. Each local
table row in the sidebar has a checkbox; tick any number and a red delete bar
appears at the top of the list with Delete / Clear. Delete confirms once, drops
them all, closes any open profile tabs for them, and refreshes -- no more
dropping tables one at a time.

Tests: the load-routing test is back to asserting the deep flatten path (DuckDB
+ flatten -> normalized tree; off -> nested; SQLite always); a test asserts the
DuckDB writer uses an Arrow bulk insert with an executemany fallback and that
the flatten path no longer uses the shallow UNNEST; and a new test guards the
multi-select delete wiring (sidebar checkboxes -> onDropMany -> api.dropTable).
Suite: 490 passing, 0 failing, 21 skipped.

build 2026-06-25.325  (v2.10.54)

Flatten on load is now DuckDB-native: the big one.

Loading a JSON file with "flatten on load" enabled no longer runs the Python
flattener (which buffered the whole file in memory and crawled -- kilobytes a
second on a multi-GB file). Instead SamQL loads the file NESTED with DuckDB's
read_json (the C++ reader -- bounded memory, no Python parse) and then flattens
it in-engine with SQL UNNEST. The whole load + flatten stays inside DuckDB, so a
file DuckDB can read in a couple of minutes flattens in about that time rather
than over days.

  - The flattened tables take over the file's name: the nested staging table is
    dropped and the root + child tables are renamed into place, so a load lands
    one clean set (root + one child per array), not a nested table plus a flat
    copy alongside it.
  - Safe fallback: if the SQL UNNEST step declines (nothing nested to explode)
    or errors, the nested table has ALREADY landed via read_json, so that is
    kept -- never worse than a nested load, and never the Python crawl again.
    (The settings toggle off still gives a single nested table, as before.)
  - SQLite loads are unchanged -- with no nested column types they still flatten
    via the Python path.

This is the same C++ read + SQL UNNEST engine added for the right-click Flatten
in the previous builds, now wired onto the load path where it matters most for
large files.

Tests: rewrote the JSON load-routing coverage -- DuckDB + flatten-on loads
nested then runs SQL UNNEST in replace mode (not the Python flattener),
flatten-off stays a single nested table, SQLite still flattens, and a declined
UNNEST keeps the nested table -- plus a check that replace mode drops the source
and renames the root into place. Suite: 489 passed, 0 failed, 21 skipped.

build 2026-06-25.324  (v2.10.53)

Flatten key handling: always generate a stable row key instead of guessing one
from column names.

The DuckDB SQL-UNNEST flatten now synthesizes a "_rowkey" for every parent
record and carries the SAME "_rowkey" column onto each child table, so you can
join or filter on one consistent column (WHERE _rowkey = ...) across the parent
and all of its children. This replaces the earlier attempt to auto-detect an
id-like column: the record key here is domain-named (e.g. a "sophis" field
nested inside an "identifier" struct) and varies from file to file, so
name-based detection was unreliable -- a deterministic generated key avoids
mislinking child rows.

Also:
  - A struct-only table (nested objects but no arrays) now flattens in-engine
    to a single keyed table -- the struct columns are left nested and stay
    queryable via dot access (identifier.sophis) -- instead of falling back to
    the slow dump + Python path. Only a truly flat table declines the fast path.
  - The wrapping-object promotion path bakes the row key in as it unnests the
    records array, so its child tables link by the same "_rowkey" too.

Note: with a generated key and array columns present, the flatten materializes
a temporary keyed copy of the table so the row number is stable across the
parent and child queries; this needs transient disk/memory roughly the size of
the table for the duration of the flatten, then the copy is dropped.

Tests: extended the SQL-UNNEST plan coverage -- the synthesized key is the same
column on the root and the children, detect-off always synthesizes, and a
struct-only table yields one keyed table with the struct kept nested. Suite:
489 passed, 0 failed, 21 skipped.

build 2026-06-25.323  (v2.10.52)

Faster JSON flatten: flatten a nested DuckDB table in-engine via SQL UNNEST
instead of dumping it back to JSON and re-parsing it in Python.

When you flatten a JSON table that lives in DuckDB, SamQL now explodes each
array column into its own child table with a set of UNNEST statements run by
the same engine that read the file. There is no Python parse and no whole-file
buffering, so a large nested table (e.g. a multi-GB derivatives export loaded
with flatten-on-load turned off) normalizes in about the time DuckDB takes to
scan it, rather than the Python flattener thrashing on it for hours.

  - Each array becomes a child table: struct arrays are expanded into columns,
    scalar arrays get a single "value" column. Child rows link to the parent by
    an auto-detected id-like key column (the record key, whose name varies from
    file to file) when one exists, or by a synthesized row key otherwise.
  - A wrapping-object shape -- a handful of rows carrying one big record array,
    e.g. {"trades":[ ... ]} -- is detected and that array promoted to the root.
  - The flatten keeps the nested source table and adds the flattened root plus
    its child tables alongside it (with uniquified names), so nothing is lost;
    drop the nested table afterward if you no longer need it.
  - Safe fallback: any unsupported shape or SQL error transparently falls back
    to the previous dump + Python flatten, so behaviour never regresses.
  - The completion notification now says which path ran -- "Flattened
    (DuckDB-native)" with the key column and table count, or "Flattened
    (Python fallback)" -- so you can see at a glance whether the fast path
    engaged or it fell back.

Tests: added coverage for id-like key auto-detection, the SQL-UNNEST plan
(root EXCLUDE of arrays, struct-array CTE expansion, scalar-array value column,
synthesized-key staging copy, child-name uniquification), and the method/key
plumbing through to the activity card. Suite: 489 passed, 0 failed, 21 skipped.

and restores the config entry exactly (removing the key again if it was absent).

load with no config override flattens into normalized tables).

Note: a config that already had the setting written to off (from an earlier
suite run) stays off until changed -- flip it back with the Settings toggle
("Turn on JSON flattening"), or remove the "flatten_json" entry from the app
config file to fall back to the on-by-default behavior.

build 2026-06-25.321  (v2.10.50)

Fix: concatenated-stream JSON lost records on a machine with the ijson
accelerator installed. The prior build asked ijson to parse multiple values from
one stream, which pulled elements out of every top-level array but silently
skipped any bare object sitting between or after arrays -- so a mixed stream
(arrays plus a trailing object) dropped those objects. The streaming reader now
lets ijson parse just the first value (the fast, bounded path for an ordinary
single array); the moment it sees a second top-level value it stops, and the
whole file is re-read with the stdlib reader that walks every value -- arrays
unwrapped element by element, bare objects included. A single array is
unaffected and still takes the fast path. (The sandbox has no ijson, so this
path is exercised by the test suite on a machine that does.)

Also clarified by a test-only change: with flatten-on-load now the default, a
large JSON file normalizes into relational tables rather than landing as the
on-disk Parquet cache view. That view is the NESTED large-file route, reached by
turning JSON flattening off (Settings) -- unchanged for CSV/Parquet, which never
flatten.

Reasoned vs tested: the concatenated/mixed reader is verified end to end in the
sandbox on the stdlib path; the ijson-then-fallback wiring runs on a machine
with ijson and should be confirmed there by re-running the suite (the two
failures this build addresses were both such machine-only paths). Suite green in
the sandbox.

build 2026-06-25.320  (v2.10.49)

Flatten JSON on load is now the default. A JSON load streams into normalized,
relational tables -- a root table plus one child table per nested array (e.g.
trades, trades_legs, trades_cashflows), with a foreign key linking children to
their parent -- instead of one table with nested columns. This is the streaming,
cancellable, heartbeating read path: it never invokes the engine's
uninterruptible whole-file JSON read and never dumps a table to JSON, so Stop
works promptly and a large load no longer trips the stall watchdog. It also
handles a concatenated-stream file (multiple top-level arrays/objects) via the
reader fix from the prior build.

The normalized tables now land in the chosen engine. For a DuckDB load the
flattener's rows are inferred to column types and batch-inserted into DuckDB
storage (previously flattening only targeted SQLite); SQLite still flattens as
before. If a DuckDB flatten hits a value that will not bind to an inferred
column type, it falls back to the nested read so the load never simply fails --
never worse than the previous behavior.

Opt back to a single nested DuckDB table with a new Settings toggle
("JSON flattening" on/off), persisted across sessions. SQLite has no nested
column types, so it always flattens regardless of the toggle. The setting is
read by the one shared load routine, so it applies uniformly to every load entry
point: drag and drop, the load modal, folder loads, and load-by-path.

Reasoned vs tested: the setting (default on, toggles, persists) and the load
routing (flatten-on to normalized tables via the flattener into the chosen
engine; off to the nested table; SQLite always flattens; and the bind-failure
fallback) are covered by new tests that run in the sandbox without a real
engine. The end-to-end DuckDB flatten insert requires DuckDB and should be
confirmed on a machine that has it by loading a JSON file and checking the
normalized tables appear. Suite is green.

build 2026-06-25.319  (v2.10.48)

Two fixes for concatenated-stream JSON (a file that is several top-level arrays
and/or objects written back to back, not one well-formed array -- the shape some
exporters emit).

1. Data loss on read (correctness). The streaming record reader special-cased a
   file starting with '[' as a single array and stopped at that array's closing
   bracket, silently discarding every value after it. A file like [..]..[..] or
   [..]{..} loaded only its first array. The reader now continues past each
   top-level value to the next one, so concatenated arrays, concatenated
   objects, NDJSON, and any mix all yield every record -- while still unwrapping
   a single (possibly multi-GB) array element-by-element with bounded memory.
   The ijson fast path now parses multiple values for the same effect. This
   affects every path that streams the raw file: the flatten loader and the
   large-array load pre-pass.

2. Stall on the flatten dump. Flattening a table whose original file is gone
   (e.g. loaded from a text bundle) dumps the table to JSON with a native
   COPY (...) TO (FORMAT JSON). That statement had no heartbeat, so a large
   nested table could run past the stall threshold with no sign of life. It now
   runs inside the same keepalive as the load statements. The build-time guard
   that checks for unguarded file-streaming statements now scans this module too
   (not just the load engine), so a dump can't silently stall in future.

Reasoned vs tested: the concatenated-stream reader is verified end to end in the
sandbox across single array, concatenated arrays, concatenated objects, mixed,
and NDJSON, plus a nested trades/legs flatten that now yields every trade and
leg across all arrays. The ijson multiple-values path cannot be exercised here
(ijson is not installed in the sandbox) and should be confirmed on a machine
that has it by checking the loaded row count matches the input. The dump
keepalive reuses the already-tested keepalive mechanism. Suite is green.

build 2026-06-25.318  (v2.10.47)

Fix: close a stall-notification gap on the large-file load path. The previous
build put the native-read keepalive (heartbeat + interrupt nudge) only around
the in-memory table read. A file at/above the on-disk threshold takes a
different route -- streamed into an on-disk columnar cache via a single COPY
(SELECT * FROM the reader) TO the cache -- and that COPY was NOT wrapped, so on
that path a multi-minute load still ran with no heartbeat and could raise the
"stalled" card. The same applied to materializing an existing view to the cache.

Both of those native statements now run inside the keepalive too, so every load
route -- in-memory table and on-disk cache -- heartbeats while the engine reads
and is nudged to stop on cancel. A lazy view creation reads nothing and needs no
guard. A new regression check inspects the engine module and fails if any
materializing native statement (a CREATE TABLE AS read, or a COPY (...) TO the
cache) is ever added without the keepalive, so this gap cannot quietly reopen.

Reasoned vs tested: the keepalive mechanism is unit-tested (it heartbeats a
worker op while a call is in flight and re-issues interrupt only after cancel);
the new check verifies every materializing statement on every load path is
wrapped. Both run in the sandbox without an engine. Suite is green.

build 2026-06-25.317  (v2.10.46)

Fix: a big JSON load now cancels promptly and no longer shows a false "stalled"
card while it reads. This addresses the case where a Stop was honored only long
after it was pressed, and the read tripped the stall watchdog in the meantime.

Root cause: the slow part of a large load is the single native engine statement
that reads the file (CREATE TABLE AS SELECT * FROM the reader). It runs entirely
in C with no way to stamp progress from Python, so a multi-minute read (a)
tripped the stall watchdog after its threshold and (b) for a raw top-level JSON
array, only observed a Stop after it had read the entire array. The pure-Python
pre-pass was already finely cancellable, but a mid-size array skipped it and was
handed straight to the engine.

Three changes:
  * A keepalive runs for the duration of that native statement: it stamps a
    heartbeat on the load operation every few seconds (so the watchdog sees it
    as alive, not hung) and, once Stop is pressed, re-issues the interrupt on a
    short interval so the read aborts at the engine's next checkpoint instead of
    only when it finishes. Beating only while a statement is actually in flight
    keeps genuine hang detection intact for everything else.
  * The streaming array pre-pass -- the cancellable, heartbeating read path --
    now engages at a modest size by default instead of a large one, so a
    mid-size array a user might want to cancel takes that path rather than the
    engine's uninterruptible raw-array read. Configurable via the same override.
  * A registry helper lets the keepalive thread refresh the heartbeat of the op
    running on the worker thread (a native call cannot beat for itself).

Reasoned vs tested: the keepalive is unit-tested with a fake connection -- it
heartbeats the worker op while a call is "in flight" and starts re-issuing
interrupt only after cancel is set -- and the cross-thread heartbeat and the new
threshold default are tested directly, all in the sandbox without a real engine.
The end-to-end engine cancel tests still pass where an engine is present. Suite
is green.

build 2026-06-25.316  (v2.10.45)

Fix: the read-phase heartbeat now fires on the accelerated (ijson) read path
too, so the stall watchdog stays quiet on boxes that have ijson installed.

The .315 heartbeat was stamped by the counting reader that wraps the file, but
that wrapper was only attached when a progress callback or cancel predicate was
supplied. The accelerated array reader is otherwise handed the raw file, so a
read with neither supplied stamped no heartbeat. The reader is now always
wrapped (it is the same wrapper already used on the progress path, so this is
not a new path for the accelerated reader), and it stamps a beat on its first
read as well as every ~256 KB -- so even a modest file beats at least once.
Cancellation is polled on every read regardless. The real load was already
unaffected (its pre-pass always supplies the cancel predicate), but the behavior
is now robust however the reader is called.

Reasoned vs tested: a direct test drives the counting reader over a >256 KB
buffer and asserts it stamps a heartbeat while forwarding bytes and raises on a
tripped cancel -- and it runs in the sandbox without the accelerated reader
installed, so it validates the exact path that a box WITH it exercises. The
mid-read cancel and streaming-reader heartbeat tests were tightened to pass the
cancel predicate exactly as the real load does. Suite is green.

build 2026-06-25.315  (v2.10.44)

Fix: Stop now cancels a JSON load while it is still reading, and a slow read no
longer raises a false "stalled" alert.

Cancel: the load's Stop already tripped the engine's cancel flag, but the
pure-Python array read only checked it once every several thousand records and
never in the middle of one record. A file of a FEW but very LARGE records (the
Sophis case: ~900 huge rows) therefore read for a long time with the flag set
and nothing looking at it, so Stop appeared to do nothing. The streaming reader
now polls for cancellation on every raw chunk read -- so a Stop aborts within a
single enormous record, not only between records -- and the pre-pass also checks
between records. A cancel during the accelerated (ijson) read path now aborts
instead of silently restarting on the tolerant reader.

False stall: the read phase emitted no progress signal, so the stall watchdog
(which flags an operation whose progress has not advanced for its threshold)
mistook a legitimately slow read for a hang and showed a "stalled" card. The
reader now stamps a lightweight heartbeat as it reads, keyed to the load
operation on its own thread, so a long read stays off the stall list. The
heartbeat is stamped only on an actual chunk read, so a genuinely blocked read
stops beating and is still correctly detected -- this quiets the false alarm
without blinding the watchdog to a real hang.

Reasoned vs tested: both behaviours are unit-tested and run in the sandbox
without a real engine -- a tripped cancel aborts mid-read of one 5 MB element
(nothing is yielded), and a multi-chunk read stamps at least one heartbeat while
every record still streams through. The existing flatten/pre-pass cancel tests
remain green; the end-to-end DuckDB cancel test still skips here and runs on your
box. Suite is green.

build 2026-06-25.314  (v2.10.43)

Fix: "Flatten JSON into tables" now appears for a DuckDB table that holds nested
data even when its source file is not named .json.

The right-click Flatten option was gated on the source file's extension ending in
.json/.ndjson/.jsonl, and the backend flatten refused a table whose source file
was anything else. But flattenability is really about nested content: the backend
already flattens any DuckDB table by dumping its STRUCT/LIST columns back out to
JSON when the source is not a JSON file. So a table whose JSON arrived as a .txt

treated as un-flattenable, the menu item was hidden, and a direct attempt errored

Now the menu offers Flatten for a DuckDB table that either came from a JSON file
or still has a nested (STRUCT / LIST / MAP / JSON) column, and the backend routes
any non-JSON source through its dump-to-JSON path instead of erroring. A flat,
non-JSON table still doesn't show the option, and SQLite tables (no JSON dumper)
still need a JSON source file.

Reasoned vs tested: the availability rule is unit-tested in the browser logic
(nested-type detection + the DuckDB/JSON/flat/SQLite cases), the backend now
flattens a table whose source file is non-JSON by dumping it (a test that runs
without a real DuckDB via the same fake dump path), and the source-shortcut
predicate is unit-tested directly. The suite is green.

build 2026-06-25.310  (v2.10.39)

Large loads now go to on-disk columnar storage instead of an in-memory table,
so memory stays bounded for the whole lifecycle -- not just while reading.

A file at or above a size threshold (512 MB by default; set SAMQL_ONDISK_MB, or
0 to turn the feature off) is now streamed into a Parquet cache and queried
through a read_parquet view, rather than materialised into an in-memory DuckDB
table. The rows never live in the engine, so a genuinely huge dataset no longer
becomes a memory-pressure point after it loads -- queries read straight from the
columnar file with column + row-group pushdown (only the columns/rows a query
needs are touched) and cached Parquet metadata for fast repeat scans, which is
the common case here (a node graph fires many queries at one source). A file
that is already Parquet is simply viewed in place (no re-copy). Smaller files
still materialise in memory, where that's fastest. If the Parquet route ever
fails for a non-cancel reason the loader falls back to the in-memory table, so
this is never worse than before. The large-JSON-array pre-pass and the
cancellation from the last builds apply on this path too.

Why Parquet and not an on-disk DuckDB database: it reuses the engine's existing,
tested Parquet-view path; it bounds memory across ingest AND queries (nothing is
materialised); Parquet is portable and version-independent, where a .duckdb file
is tied to the engine version; and object-cached metadata plus pushdown make
repeat queries fast. An on-disk DuckDB table can edge it out on some repeated
complex queries but needs attach/versioning machinery for a marginal gain. To
check the trade-off on real data there's a new tools/bench_large_load.py that
loads a file three ways -- in-memory, Parquet view, and on-disk DuckDB -- each in
its own process, and reports load time, a sample query time, and peak memory, so
the choice can be validated per machine and file.

Reasoned vs tested: the size threshold and its off switch are unit-tested and
run everywhere. The end-to-end large load landing as a Parquet cache view --
queryable, right rows and columns, backed by a Parquet file rather than an
in-memory copy -- is covered by a test that runs wherever DuckDB is installed
and skips in the sandbox. The COPY-to-Parquet-then-view path reuses the same
statements the convert-to-Parquet feature already exercises. The benchmark's
own logic (reader selection, the array pre-pass, memory measurement) is
smoke-checked here; its DuckDB runs happen on your machine. The suite is green.

  * Spreadsheet read. Loading a big .xlsx read every row through openpyxl in a

Cancelling a large JSON load now works while it's still reading, and the

Two related changes to the .307 large-JSON-array streaming:

build 2026-06-25.307  (v2.10.36)

Large single JSON arrays now stream instead of running out of memory.

A JSON file that is one big top-level array -- [ {...}, {...}, ... ] -- is the
one shape DuckDB's JSON reader has to buffer essentially whole: unlike
newline-delimited JSON, it can't stream the elements or spill them, so on a
multi-GB array it exhausts the memory limit before a single row lands ("Out of
Memory Error: failed to allocate ... while reading the file"). When a load hits
a JSON file at or above a size threshold (128 MB by default; set
SAMQL_JSON_STREAM_MB to change it) and it turns out to be a single top-level
array, the loader now rewrites it to newline-delimited JSON first, in a
streaming pass that holds only a small read buffer no matter how big the file
is, and points DuckDB at that instead. DuckDB then streams it row by row and
spills to its temp directory as usual. The element split is done by the
standard library's JSON decoder, so nested objects, arrays, escaped quotes and
the like are handled exactly; the temp file is cleaned up once the table is
built. Files below the threshold, newline-delimited files, and single-object
files are untouched -- they already load fine. The resulting table shows the
object keys as columns, same as any other JSON load.

This pairs with the existing memory safeguards (the auto-sized DuckDB memory
limit, which an admin can override with SAMQL_DUCKDB_MEMORY_GB, plus spill to a
managed temp directory): the limit and spill handle big tables once they are
loaded, and this handles getting an oversized array in without blowing the
limit during the read itself.

Reasoned vs tested: the streaming converter is unit-tested directly, including
the boundary cases a naive splitter gets wrong -- a value or a number that
straddles a read-buffer boundary, strings that contain brackets/braces/commas,
escaped quotes and backslashes, a byte-order mark, and non-array inputs that
must be left alone -- run at deliberately tiny buffer sizes to force refills
everywhere. The end-to-end DuckDB load of a top-level array through this path is
covered by a test that runs wherever DuckDB is installed (it skips in the CI
sandbox, which has no DuckDB). The suite is green.

build 2026-06-25.306  (v2.10.35)

Two things: NDJSON loaded into DuckDB shows real column headers, and the query
editor gets a right-click "SQL functions" menu.

When DuckDB loads a JSON or NDJSON file whose rows come back as a single
structured column -- most often NDJSON whose every line is a one-element array
wrapping an object, which lands as one opaque column of "list of struct" -- the

build 2026-06-25.304  (v2.10.33)

Load: very large NDJSON files read faster on the DuckDB engine -- the format

When DuckDB loads a newline-delimited JSON file (a .ndjson or .jsonl), it now
reads it with the format stated explicitly instead of auto-detecting, so DuckDB

connection caps its memory, spills to a managed temp directory, runs
multithreaded, and does not preserve input order, so huge loads already stream
out of core rather than filling RAM. Materializing the file with this kind of
load already lands it in DuckDB's columnar storage, so there is no separate
intermediate file -- that round-trip only helps when the same source is read
repeatedly.

Reasoned vs tested: the reader selection (newline-delimited for NDJSON,
auto-detect for other JSON, the tolerant retries, and the per-object size cap)
is unit-tested with no engine required, and the end-to-end load through the

suite is green. The actual speed-up on a multi-GB file is reasoned, not

not import any GUI toolkit; the only window is your browser.)

The executable icon, the favicon and manifest the server serves for the browser
tab, and the data engine are all unchanged. Rebuild the executable to pick this
up; the frontend is unaffected.

Reasoned vs tested: the spec keeping a console and building no splash, and the
source dropping the no-console plumbing (stream redirect, fatal dialog) and the

build 2026-06-25.301  (v2.10.30)

Three improvements: deeper JSON flattening, memory-bounded API loads, and a
pivot that collapses to its subtotals.

JSON flattening now handles arrays nested three or more levels deep -- they
explode into chained child tables (parent, child, child items, ...) instead of
being stringified at the third level, so the inner values stay queryable. A
depth cap keeps a pathologically deep document from overflowing the parser
stack: past the cap a still-nested value is kept verbatim rather than crashing.
A field whose type differs between records (sometimes a scalar, sometimes an
object) stays lossless, and one- and two-level shapes are byte-for-byte
unchanged.

Loading an API response into SQLite is now memory-bounded. The records are
streamed straight from the spooled response into the flattener, which spills its
per-table row buffers to disk past a threshold, so neither the parsed records
nor the flattened rows are all held in memory at once -- the same way file loads
already work, and the way the DuckDB path already reads the file directly. A
2xx response that turns out to hold no records still gives a clean "no records"
message instead of a parser error.

In a pivot with subtotals turned on, collapsing a nested row group now shows
that group's rolled-up subtotal values on the collapsed line -- the Excel /
Tableau "collapse to subtotal" behaviour -- instead of blanking the row and
showing only a count. Expanding restores the detail rows.

Reasoned vs tested: the flattening and API-load changes are covered by new tests
(deep and mixed-type arrays plus the depth cap; a streamed-and-spilled API load
with a nested child table, a records-path, and an empty response) and the full
suite is green. The pivot collapse is verified by a source check and is
type-checked; the on-screen behaviour over the app window is reasoned, not run
here.

build 2026-06-25.300  (v2.10.29)

Fix: a changed logo / icon now actually shows up after a rebuild.

Two things were keeping a stale icon on screen. First, the build scripts ran
the packager without a clean step, so it could reuse its build cache and embed
the previous icon, splash or bundled asset; they now force a clean rebuild
(--clean) and clear the previous build/ and dist/ directories first. (The
frontend was already rebuilt each time, so a changed frontend/public app icon
was being copied -- the gap was the packager's own cache.)

Second, the app window's favicon -- which is its Windows taskbar icon -- was
served with a "cache for a day" header. Once the window moved to a persistent
browser profile (the state-persistence fix), that header meant the browser kept
showing the previously cached logo after a rebuild. It is now served no-store,
so the window refetches the icon on each launch and a new one appears straight
away. A real bundled app icon is read and served directly (still overridable by
dropping a PNG into frontend/public), also no-store.

If a stale icon still lingers, it is a client-side cache a rebuild cannot touch:
clear the SamQL UI profile once (under the per-user app-data folder) to drop a
cached favicon, and note that the program file's own icon in the file manager
is cached separately by the OS shell.

Reasoned vs tested: the build scripts using a clean rebuild, and the icon being
served no-store with the drop-in override, are unit-tested. That the rebuilt
logo actually appears -- and clearing the OS-level icon caches -- can only be
confirmed on a real Windows build.

build 2026-06-25.294  (v2.10.23)

Packaging: the source bundle is now email-safe (defanged); the extractor
un-defangs it on import. The app code is unchanged from .293 -- this round is
packaging plus the extractor plus a test.

Some email and URL gateways flag samql_full_source.txt as "containing an
executable url link". The trigger is bare executable-style filename tokens read
as links -- SamQL[.]exe, signtool[.]exe, chrome[.]exe, msedge[.]exe, build[.]ps1,
esbuild[.]cmd and the like -- not any URL that actually points to an executable
(there are none). To get the bundle through a text-only email path it is now
shipped "defanged": a bracketed dot is inserted in front of executable-style
extensions ([.]exe, [.]dll, [.]msi, [.]bat, [.]cmd, [.]scr, [.]vbs, [.]ps1, [.]jar), so for
example SamQL[.]exe is carried with a bracketed dot before "exe". The match is
boundary-anchored, so look-alikes such as ".exec" and ".execute" are left
untouched, and the real source never contains a bracketed dot, so the
transformation is exact.

Expand-SamQL[.]ps1 reverses it: before it splits the bundle on the "===== FILE:"
headers it does one global swap of the bracketed-dot token back to a plain dot,
so the reconstructed tree is byte-for-byte the real source. That swap is a
no-op on a bundle that was never defanged, so the same extractor works on
either -- but the previous extractor would write broken files from a defanged
bundle, so use the updated one. To send everything as plain text, email the
defanged samql_full_source.txt and Expand-SamQL[.]ps1.txt (saved back with a [.]ps1
extension), then run the extractor.

A file:///etc/passwd string remains in the bundle: it is a fixture for the test
that the API loader rejects non-http(s) URL schemes, it is not executable, and
it was not what the gateway flagged.

Reasoned vs tested: the defang / un-defang round-trip and the look-alike guard
are unit-tested, and the extractor is source-guarded to carry the un-defang
step. As always, PyInstaller actually producing the exe, the Chrome/Edge app
window opening, and the PowerShell extractor running on a real bundle cannot
run in this sandbox; confirm on a real Windows/Citrix box.

build 2026-06-25.290  (v2.10.19)

Iterator + API node: a nested API node now pins the flow's engine (completes the .289 fix).

Build .289 corrected engine selection for a top-level API node, but the
iterator+API-node failure ("The group node couldn't run: OperationalError: no
such table: __nbapi_...") kept happening, because that was the wrong case. When
an API node is dragged *inside* an iterator -- the normal way to use it -- the
iterator runs as a container: it wraps its child nodes in a synthetic "group"
node and runs that group once per row. The API node is therefore nested in the
group's children, not a top-level node.

_flow_engine_target -- which decides the single engine a flow runs on -- only
scanned the graph's top-level nodes. The nested API node was invisible to it, so
nothing pinned the engine and the flow defaulted to SQLite, while the API node's
hidden table had been loaded into DuckDB (the default engine when DuckDB is
installed). The group's "SELECT * FROM __nbapi_..." then ran on SQLite and the
table wasn't there.

The fix makes _flow_engine_target descend into group and iterator children when
choosing the engine, applying the same logic used for top-level nodes: a nested
API node is routed to the engine the fetch actually loaded it into (the .289
change), and a nested file/input/SQL node pins the engine the same way it would
at the top level. The group now runs on the engine that holds the data, and the
body reads its table.

This does not change how any flow runs on success or how single-engine flows
behave; it only widens engine selection to see inputs nested inside containers.
The loop and ${variable} substitution were never involved -- the error already
showed the date resolving each pass.

Reasoned vs tested: covered by a new test asserting a group (and an iterator)
with a nested API node recorded as living in DuckDB routes the flow to DuckDB,
plus a fallback (a group with no engine-pinning child stays local). The
container-iterator path with a child API node is also exercised end-to-end on
SQLite in the suite; the DuckDB end-to-end run is confirmed on the real
Windows/Citrix build, where DuckDB is present.

build 2026-06-25.289  (v2.10.18)

Iterator + API node: read the API node's data from the engine it loaded into.

An iterator (or while loop) whose body contained an API node could fail every
pass with "The group node couldn't run: OperationalError: no such table:
__nbapi_..." even though the fetch succeeded. The hidden table the API node
loads its response into is created in whichever engine is the default for new
data -- DuckDB whenever it is installed -- but the flow that reads it was being
routed to SQLite, so the body's "SELECT * FROM __nbapi_..." looked for a DuckDB
table in SQLite and reported it missing.

The cause: a flow runs on a single engine, chosen by _flow_engine_target from
its input tables. For an API node it read the engine out of the cached catalog,
and the freshly-created hidden table was not reflected there at that instant
inside an iterator pass, so the lookup came back empty and the flow defaulted to
SQLite. The data was in DuckDB the whole time.

The fix makes _flow_engine_target trust the engine the fetch actually recorded
for the node (the API-node registry tracks, per node, the engine its table and
error table live in) rather than re-deriving it from the catalog cache. When no
fetch has run for a node it still falls back to the catalog, so the manual
(non-iterator) path is unchanged. This routes the flow to the engine that holds
the data, and the body reads its table.

This does not change what loads on a successful fetch or how any single-engine
flow runs; it only corrects engine selection when an API node's hidden table
is not yet visible in the cache. The loop and ${variable} substitution were
never the problem -- the error already showed the date resolving.

Reasoned vs tested: covered by a new test that records an API node's table as
living in DuckDB while leaving it absent from both cached catalogs (the bug
condition) and asserts the flow targets DuckDB, plus a fallback case (an
un-fetched node still resolves to the local engine). The end-to-end iterator +
API-node-on-DuckDB path itself is exercised on the real Windows/Citrix build,
where DuckDB is present.

build 2026-06-25.288  (v2.10.17)

API node: an actionable error when an endpoint doesn't return JSON.

An API node (including each pass of an iterator or while loop) that fetched an
endpoint returning something other than JSON -- an HTML login or error page,
plain text, or an empty body -- used to fail with a raw "JSONDecodeError:
Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)", which says nothing about what
actually came back. That bubbled up verbatim as an iterator pass error, so a
corporate endpoint quietly redirecting to a sign-in page looked like a parser
bug.

The streaming fetch path (the one iterator and while passes use) now catches a
body that won't parse and reports the HTTP status, the content-type, and a short
snippet of what arrived -- for example: "The endpoint did not return JSON (HTTP
200, text/html). Got this instead: '<!DOCTYPE html>...'. Check the URL and any
required auth/headers (a corporate endpoint often returns an HTML login page),
or set a Records path if the JSON is nested." An empty 2xx body is reported
plainly as an empty response instead of failing to parse "". The in-memory
fetch_json path (preview and paginated fetches) got the same wording for
consistency.

This is a diagnostics-only change: it does not alter what loads on a successful
fetch, only the message shown when a response can't be read as JSON. The
variable substitution and the loop itself were never the problem -- the error
already showed the date resolving correctly.

Reasoned vs tested: covered by a new test that drives the loader's streaming
path with an injected spooler returning an HTML page and an empty body, and
asserts a human error (status + content-type + snippet) with no raw
JSONDecodeError leaking.

build 2026-06-25.287  (v2.10.16)

Pivot result grid: collapse / expand nested row groups.

When a pivot has more than one row dimension, each non-leaf row-dimension cell
now carries a small chevron. Clicking it folds that group's child rows into a
single representative row -- the parent value stays visible with a count of how
many rows are hidden, and the deeper dimensions and the value cells are blanked.
Click again to expand. Each group is independent, so you can collapse one parent
to get it out of the way while leaving another fully expanded, which is the point
when two parents each have a long list of children. Collapse works at every
nesting level (the shallowest collapsed ancestor wins), and the collapsed state
resets whenever the pivot's shape changes.

Because the row nesting is only contiguous while the grid is in dimension order,
collapse is offered only then; sorting by a value column temporarily turns the
chevrons off (sorting by a dimension keeps them). The grid is shared, so this
lands in both the SQL IDE and the Journal pivot modals.

Honest scope note: a collapsed parent shows a count of hidden rows, not an
aggregated subtotal. Re-aggregating client-side would be wrong for averages
(avg-of-avgs) without carrying per-group weights, so true subtotals are left as a
separate follow-up rather than shipped incorrectly.

Reasoned vs tested: source-guarded + tsc-gated (no node_modules in the sandbox).
The suite asserts the collapse state, the child-suppression display model, the
chevron control and glyphs, the hidden-row count, the value-sort gate, the
shape-change reset, and that the shared panel is used in both views.

Activity panel: move Cancel-all into the task tray, off the live card.

The catch-all Cancel-all button used to sit on the live "Working" card in the
SERVER section, where it overlapped the status text whenever a load was running.

tasks" header and above the task cards -- and it appears whenever a task is
running.

moved.

Reasoned vs tested: source-guarded + tsc-gated (no node_modules in the sandbox).
The suite asserts the Working-card Stop and all of its onStop wiring are gone,
and that Cancel-all is now a tray row wired to api.cancelAll, shown whenever a
background task is running.

Node config: move the help button beside the name, and make it a lightbulb.

In the Node view's config panel the help button used to sit immediately next to

build 2026-06-25.283  (v2.10.12)

Pivot grid: sortable + resizable columns, and a clearer red remove button.

The pivot result grid now sorts and resizes. Click a column header to sort by
that column -- ascending, then descending, then off, with an arrow marking the
active column. Drag the right edge of any header to resize it. Column widths are
measured from the natural layout the first time a pivot renders and then become
draggable, so resizing is precise without changing how a fresh pivot looks. Both
land in the SQL IDE and the Journal, because the two share one pivot panel.

The field-chip remove button -- the x on each Rows, Columns, Summarize and
Filters field -- is now a clear red at rest and goes solid red on hover. It was
a faint grey before and easy to miss.

Reasoned vs tested: source-guarded + tsc-gated (no node_modules in the sandbox).

shared panel feeds both surfaces; the actual click-to-sort and drag-to-resize
behavior needs a real build.

build 2026-06-25.282  (v2.10.11)

Nodebook: drop the Run-all progress bar; Run simply flips to Stop.

Removed the small determinate progress bar that sat beside the Run button in the
workflow toolbar and counted finished terminals (e.g. "1/2"). Because most
workflows finish almost instantly, the bar would flash in and shove the
neighbouring toolbar buttons sideways for a fraction of a second, which made the
Run button look like it jumped for no reason. The button alone now carries the
state: it reads Run, and flips to a red Stop while a workflow is running.

Cancellation is unchanged. Stop still calls the same cancelRun path, and the
per-node abort + engine interrupt and the "Run all cancelled" toast all remain.
Only the progress display and its client-side terminal-counting state were
removed, along with the now-orphaned styles -- the kept terminal count still
feeds the cancellation summary.

Reasoned vs tested: source-guarded + tsc-gated (no node_modules in the sandbox).
The suite now asserts the Node view renders no progress bar and keeps the
Run/Stop toggle wired to cancelRun, rather than the reverse.

build 2026-06-25.281  (v2.10.10)

Every temporary artifact now lives in the swept per-process directory.

Closes a temp-file leak that could survive a truly hard kill. SamQL keeps all
its scratch files under one per-process directory that a clean exit deletes and
the next startup sweeps if the process died -- but a handful of temp artifacts
were being created directly in the system temp root instead, where that sweep
never looked. On a hard kill (SIGKILL, power loss, force-terminate -- no
shutdown handler runs), those leaked for good.

Routed every remaining temp file into the per-process directory: the disk-backed
database, the JSON-flatten spill, the export spill, the lineage workbook, the
Excel sheet-name peek, and persistent uploads. Each now passes an explicit
target directory, with a couple of clearly-marked last-resort fallbacks for the
rare case where the per-process directory itself can't be created.

Two robustness fixes came with it. The flatten spill is now torn down with a
recursive remove rather than a plain directory remove, which previously left the
directory behind if any spill file lingered. And the startup sweep now also
scans the system temp root for orphaned SamQL files by age -- so leftovers from
earlier builds get reclaimed on upgrade, not just going forward.

A new test enforces the invariant directly: no temp-creation site may omit its
target directory, and the temp-root sweep is exercised end to end.

Reasoned vs tested: the routing and the new sweep are covered by the suite. The
disk-DB, export and lineage paths that require DuckDB or openpyxl are guarded
statically in the sandbox; their on-disk write behavior is otherwise unchanged.

build 2026-06-25.280  (v2.10.9)

A second pass of micro-animations.

Five more, on the same rules as the first batch -- transform/opacity only,
one-shot, and all behind the reduced-motion guard. Nodes scale in when they are
placed and lift slightly while dragged; toasts grow a thin countdown bar that
