Two details worth noting. The tab underline is measured -- it reads the active
tab's position -- and it rides inside the scrolling tab strip, so it stays
aligned even with many tabs scrolled off-screen. And because canvas nodes are
positioned with left/top rather than a transform, the scale lift never fights
the drag: dragging itself stays instant.

Everything still switches off under the reduced-motion guard, either the OS
"reduce motion" setting or the Settings toggle.

Reasoned vs tested: source-guarded + tsc-gated (the sandbox has no node_modules
to render the UI). The keyframes, the underline's measure-and-position effect,
the run-success flash trigger, and the toast bar are all checked in the suite;

build 2026-06-25.279  (v2.10.8)

Subtle one-shot animations, behind a reduced-motion guard.

A first pass of small, event-driven motion -- all on transform/opacity so it
stays cheap over Citrix. Right-click menus grow from near the cursor (fade +
scale); modals fade and rise in instead of snapping; buttons get a slight
press-scale on click; the selected node's ring eases in rather than hard-
switching; and toasts now slide out as well as in. Nothing continuous was added

system's "reduce motion" setting, and there is a new "Reduce motion" toggle in
Settings. When on, a body class zeroes every animation and transition, so a slow
remote session can turn it all off; the choice persists across restarts.

to render the UI). The keyframes, the guard (media query + body class), the

build 2026-06-25.276  (v2.10.5)

A Stop on the live activity card -- halt a running load (or anything) from the card that shows it.

The "Working" card in the stat popover and the Activity modal shows what the
server is doing right now ("Loading FTRG", a busy DuckDB, and so on), but a load
had no cancel anywhere: loads register in the operation registry without a run
id, so they never qualified for the inline x added in .274, and they aren't run
through the per-job tray cards either. So you could watch a load grind without a
way to stop it short of resetting the server.

The card now carries a Stop whenever something is actually running, wired to the
same global cancel-all the Nodebook Stop uses: it interrupts every engine (which
aborts an in-flight load / query / read) and flags every background job. It
appears only while there is real work in flight and is hidden during session
restore, which stays uncancellable by design (interrupting a rebuild mid-way
would leave tables half-built). This complements, rather than replaces, the
per-op x on cancellable runs and the per-card cancel on tray jobs -- it is the
catch-all for work that has no targetable run id of its own, the loads chief
among them.

Reasoned vs tested: the Stop's gating (shown when an op is registered or an
engine is busy, hidden when idle or restoring) and its wiring to cancel-all in
both surfaces are tsc-gated + source-guarded -- the sandbox has no node_modules
to run the UI live. The cancel-all path itself is the same engine-interrupt the
Nodebook Stop already uses, exercised on the live SQLite engine.

build 2026-06-25.275  (v2.10.4)

Cancel the IDE & result analytics from the activity panel and popover.

The in-IDE reconcile (and its drilldown and field profile), the result pivot,
the chart-data builder, and a single-field profile used to run straight on the
engine with no run id, so nothing but the global cancel-all could reach them,
and not cleanly. They now run through the same registered run-rail their
Nodebook twins already use: each gets a run id, a stall-watchdog entry, and the
inline x in the ACTIVE OPERATIONS table and the stat popover for free. Clicking
it routes through cancel_query, whose engine interrupt aborts the in-flight
statement; the op then returns a cancel result instead of an error. The
Nodebook versions of these were already cancellable -- this closes the gap on
the IDE / result side.

Result export is deliberately left out of this pass. It is not a single engine
statement but a Python loop writing rows straight to the output file, so an
engine interrupt cannot stop it -- wrapping it would have shipped a cancel
button that did nothing and risked a half-written file. Making export
cancellable needs a per-row cancel check threaded through the CSV / JSON / XLSX
/ Parquet writers plus partial-file cleanup, which is its own focused follow-up.

Reasoned vs tested: _run_op's behaviour is unit-tested live -- it registers a
visible, cancellable op for the duration of the call, generates a run id when
the caller passes none, and returns the cancel sentinel (even when the callee
swallowed the interrupt) rather than reporting a user cancel as success. The
cancellation itself is the same engine-interrupt path as Stop, exercised on the
live SQLite engine; the six handlers are source-guarded to route through it
(and export guarded to stay out). No frontend change was needed -- the inline x
shipped in .274 renders any registered cancellable op -- so this round is
backend-only.

build 2026-06-25.274  (v2.10.3)

Cancel in-flight operations from the activity panel and the stat popover.

The ACTIVE OPERATIONS table in the Activity & connections modal was read-only:
a foreground query, a Nodebook / Node flow, an iterator / while loop, a column
profile, a save-as-table, a change-column-type, or a connector import (REST
fetch / SQL Server) showed there with no way to stop it from that surface.
Each such row now carries an inline Cancel (x) that hits the existing per-run
cancel rail (POST /api/query/{id}/cancel -> cancel_query), the same mechanism
the IDE and Nodebook Stop buttons already use.

The stat (memory) popover now lists those same cancellable runs under the
server status, each with the same one-click cancel, so a stray query or
profile can be stopped without opening the modal -- alongside the existing
background-task cards (load / folder / HDFS / convert / flatten).

An operation shows a cancel control only when it runs under a real run id the
system can target. Foreground runs and in-IDE background ops register under
their query id and are cancellable; a background load streams under a
generated id and is cancelled from its own tray card instead (not doubled
here); session restore after a reset has no run id and stays uncancellable by
design -- it is internal recovery, not a user operation, so it shows no
cancel button.

Reasoned vs tested: the per-op cancellable flag is unit-tested live (an op
begun under an explicit run id is cancellable; one without is not). The inline
cancel in the modal and the run list in the popover are tsc-gated +
source-guarded (no node_modules in the sandbox). Cancellation stays
best-effort for non-engine work (REST fetch / SQL Server), consistent with
Stop -- it flags the run and interrupts the engines, and the op unwinds at its
next checkpoint.

build 2026-06-25.273  (v2.10.2)

Flatten: cancellable, progressing, and no more false stall.

The in-place JSON flatten now runs as a background job, so it shows up as a
card (with a live row count) in the activity tray + the stat popover, with a
Cancel X -- and Cancel all / the Nodebook Stop reach it too. Previously it
ran as a request that blocked until the (possibly long) flatten finished and
gave no way to stop it.

Fixed the false "stall detected" on a long flatten. The flatten now stamps
the progress registry as it streams records, so the watchdog no longer
mistakes a working flatten for a hang once it passes the stall threshold, and
its live row count shows on the dashboard. (The big-JSON flatten seen in
testing was not actually broken -- it was still progressing but reporting
nothing, so the watchdog flagged it ~90s in and the row count sat at 0.)

Honest progress instead of a bar frozen at 0%. An operation that can't report
incremental progress now shows a live spinner rather than a 0%-stuck bar. A
DuckDB "copy into a table" load is a single atomic COPY and DuckDB's fast
native reader doesn't expose per-row progress, so there is no true percentage
to show; the flatten shows a climbing row count + spinner because the
streamed JSON's record total isn't known up front. (Chunked SQLite loads and
HDFS downloads still show a real byte bar once bytes start moving.)

Reasoned vs tested: the flatten job lifecycle + cancel, the heartbeat fix,
and the progress-mode logic are live-tested on SQLite + the fake-engine
harness; the DuckDB COPY itself and the frontend wiring are tsc-gated +
source-guarded (no DuckDB / node_modules in the sandbox).

Activity tray + global Stop.

The per-load progress modal is gone. Long loads, folder loads, HDFS

build 2026-06-25.270  (v2.9.1)

Activity-tray backend foundation (concurrent background tasks).

Groundwork for moving long tasks off blocking modals into one activity
tray. All additive + internal -- the UI still uses the existing progress
modals until the tray lands, so there is no visible change yet.

- A unified task feed (GET /api/tasks) normalizes every background job --
  load / folder / multipart / convert / flatten, and now API + iterator
  runs -- into one card shape with an honest progress mode (bytes when a
  size is known, a spinner for the atomic Parquet COPY, step count where a
  pass count exists). It is the single list the tray will poll, and it
  re-discovers still-running work after a reload.

- A single-owner FIFO engine slot serializes background jobs' ENGINE
  phases (a load's CREATE TABLE, a convert's COPY) while leaving their IO
  phases (an HDFS download, a JSON read) free to overlap. Pure-engine jobs
  queue behind each other and auto-advance; foreground SELECTs don't use
  the slot (they contend on the engine lock as before), so a plain query
  never becomes a task.

- Per-card cancellation is scoped: a card's X interrupts the engine only
  when that job currently owns the slot. A queued job, or one still
  downloading, cancels cooperatively -- so cancelling one card never
  aborts another task's engine work. A new scoped run-cancel flag stops an
  iterator / API run's loop between passes without the global Stop hammer.

- API and iterator runs can now run in the background and persist their
  output as a real table: an iterator builds its accumulator table; an API
  run materializes its node output into a table (overwriting that run's
  own table on re-run). The synchronous endpoints stay for foreground
  previews.

Reasoned-vs-tested: the FIFO/auto-advance/cancel-while-queued behavior is
live-tested with real threads; two concurrent loads finish without
deadlock; an iterator and an API run each go end-to-end through the
job + slot path and create their table -- all on SQLite. The real DuckDB
COPY through the slot, and a real networked API fetch, remain
DuckDB-/network-gated and source-guarded in the sandbox.

build 2026-06-25.269  (v2.9.0)

Convert a table to columnar Parquet on demand (faster repeat queries).

A file-backed DuckDB view -- e.g. a CSV or JSON loaded as a zero-copy
view, or one streamed in from HDFS -- re-parses its text on every scan.
Right-click such a table and choose "Convert to Parquet (faster
queries)" to re-store it as a Parquet file in place: repeat queries then
get DuckDB's column + row-group pushdown instead of re-reading the text.
The menu item only appears for file-backed CSV/TSV/JSON views on the
DuckDB engine (already-Parquet and non-file tables are skipped), and the
backend re-checks before doing any work.

The conversion runs on the shared load job rail, so the progress window's
Cancel / X stop it: the COPY is a single statement, so a Stop interrupts
it through the engine (the same interrupt_loads path a load cancel uses)
and a cooperative pre-check catches a cancel that lands first. On cancel
or error the partial Parquet is deleted and the original view is left
exactly as it was -- nothing is re-pointed until the COPY finishes. The
Parquet lands in this run's temp dir, so dropping the table later cleans
it up, and the old CSV/JSON temp is removed once the swap succeeds.

DuckDB-only: without DuckDB the action is hidden and the endpoint returns
a clean "needs the DuckDB engine" 400. Honest reasoned-vs-tested note --
the gating, view re-point, temp cleanup, and cancel/partial-cleanup
behaviour are covered live with a fake engine; the real DuckDB COPY (and
its mid-statement interrupt) is DuckDB-gated and source-guarded in the
sandbox, exercised end to end only on the real Windows/Citrix box.

build 2026-06-25.258  (v2.4.10)

JSON flatten (SQLite) now actually cancels. Pressing Stop while a JSON
file was loading/flattening said "Canceling", then stalled while SQLite
finished flattening the whole file anyway. Three structural fixes:

- The flattener was SWALLOWING the cancel. JSONFlattener._emit routed its
  progress callback through `except Exception: pass`, and the load job's
  cancel signal is a LoadCancelled exception raised by that callback --
  which is an Exception, so it got swallowed and the parse phase ran to
  completion. _emit now re-raises a LoadCancelled (matched by class name to
  avoid a circular import) and only swallows genuine progress-report errors.
- The table-write phase was uninterruptible. db.add_table_streaming never
  calls back, so a Stop pressed after parsing (while rows were being
  inserted) wasn't seen until the whole table was written. load_json now
  re-pings the progress callback every 5000 rows while streaming rows into
  the table, so cancellation (and the progress bar) are live there too.
- The flatten ACTION (flatten a loaded table) passed no progress callback
  at all, so it had no cancel hook even after the above. flatten_json now
  passes a progress callback that raises on cancel, and drops any partial
  tables a mid-write cancel leaves behind (the file-load jobs already did
  this clean-up; the action now matches).

Net: Stop during a JSON load/flatten aborts promptly in both the parse and
the write phases, and the partially-written tables are removed -- instead
of "Canceling" hanging while the flatten completes. The earlier flatten
cancellation work (start-check + engine interrupt) could not help here
because the work is Python-side JSON flattening, not an interruptible SQL
statement; this makes it cooperative instead.

Tested: a unit test asserts the flattener no longer swallows a cancel
raised by its progress callback, and an end-to-end test asserts load_json
aborts mid-flatten when the callback signals cancel (6k-record file, SQLite
engine). Suite 418 passing. DuckDB JSON load is a single read_json call
(already interruptible / not affected).

build 2026-06-25.257  (v2.4.9)

Iterator / while loops: per-pass API fetch is now cooperatively
cancellable.

- Each pass's API-node fetch (and any API node nested inside a container
  iterator's children) now shares the run's cancel check: the run's
  query_id is threaded into fetch_api_node via should_cancel, so hitting
  Stop while a pass is mid-fetch aborts between pages / download chunks
  instead of waiting out the 60s HTTP timeout before the loop's next
  between-pass cancel check. Pure-SQL passes were already immediate (the
  engine interrupt); this closes the API-fetch gap.
- It shares the run's cancel check WITHOUT clobbering the run's
  registration. fetch_api_node only registers / unregisters a run id when
  it OWNS that run (a standalone API node); when a caller (an iterator /
  while pass) already owns the run and passes should_cancel, the fetch
  reuses it and skips register/unregister -- otherwise its unregister
  would discard the run's cancel flag and end the loop's progress entry
  the moment a pass returned. (own_run guard.)

On the iterator timeout question: there is deliberately NO frontend
wall-clock timeout on an iterator / while run -- /api/iterator/run and
/api/while/run are in the unbounded-endpoint set (see build .256). A loop
is legitimately long, so a wall-clock cap would wrongly kill valid runs.
The loop sends no caller signal, so it still sits in the in-flight set and
is aborted by Stop / window-close; between that, the cooperative
between-pass cancel checks, and the per-pass backstops (engine interrupt
for SQL, the 60s HTTP timeout for fetches -- now also cooperative), it is
fully cancellable without a timer. A wedged LOCAL engine query inside a
pass is unbounded-but-cancellable, exactly like a wedged main query.

Tested: SQLite + the cooperative register/own-run bookkeeping (new test
asserts a per-pass fetch does not discard the run's cancel flag, and a
standalone fetch still clears its own). DuckDB reasoned. Suite 416 passing.

build 2026-06-25.256  (v2.4.8)

Cancellation overhaul, part 4 of 4 -- timeout backstops. A wedged socket can no
longer leave a request unsettled forever (which would tie up the browser's
per-host connection pool and stall the UI even when the user never pressed
Stop). This completes the overhaul (parts 1-3 added the cancel paths; part 4
bounds the calls that no cancel ever reached).

Frontend: every no-signal request is now bounded
  • jsonFetch resolves an effective timeout: a caller signal means the caller
    owns cancellation (no cap); an explicit timeoutMs wins (0 = deliberately
    unbounded); a data-volume endpoint is unbounded; otherwise a 3-minute
    default backstop applies. Previously ~68 of ~75 POSTs had no timeout and
    could hang indefinitely.
  • Data-volume endpoints opt out of the backstop (their runtime scales with the
    user's data and is legitimately long): nodeflow run / write / export /
    export-many / reconcile / validate / chart / browse, iterator + while loops,
    the multi-page API node fetch, reconcile (+ drill-in / profile), catalog
    import, run-tests, IDE chart + pivot aggregation, and the synchronous file
    loads. These remain cancellable via Stop / window-close / abortInflight.
  • Frequent, fixed-size calls (schema column inspection, metadata, mutations,
    status, paging, job-starts, cancels) keep the backstop -- exactly the calls
    where a hang is a bug and a timeout is the right recovery.

Backend: confirmed already bounded (no change needed, documented here)
  • HTTP API fetch: the urllib fetcher already applies a 60s per-request
    timeout, so a black-hole endpoint raises rather than hanging mid-read.
  • SQL Server: connect is bounded by login_timeout (15s) and catalog/table
    browse by meta_timeout; the statement timeout stays unbounded on purpose
    because a long query is cancellable (part 3, cursor.cancel).
  • HDFS: the WebHDFS client sets a 20s socket timeout on every urlopen, which
    also bounds a wedged mid-stream chunk read in the file fetch loop.

Honesty
  • The 3-minute default is a backstop, not the primary recovery -- Stop, the
    window-close cancels, and Reset server act immediately. It only matters when
    the user does nothing and a "should be quick" call wedged.
  • A data-volume op that genuinely runs longer than any cancel and wedges is
    bounded by the relevant server-side socket timeout above, not by a frontend
    wall-clock cap (so a legitimately long flow/reconcile is never cut off).

Tests (TDD): a frontend guard asserts the default backstop exists, jsonFetch
resolves the effective timeout (signal / explicit / unbounded-path / default),
the data-volume endpoints opt out, reconcile sub-ops are unbounded, and the
schema-inspect calls stay backstopped. Suite: 415 passed, 0 failed, 15 skipped.
tsc clean on the changed file.

The cancellation overhaul is complete: Stop and window-close are hard kills
everywhere (parts 1-2), remote REST/SQL Server I/O is cancellable (part 3), and
nothing can hang the UI indefinitely (part 4).

build 2026-06-25.253  (v2.4.5)

Cancellation overhaul, part 1 of N -- the Nodebook. Stop is now a hard kill:
nothing associated with a run keeps going after you press it.

Stop cancels the WHOLE workflow, client + server
  • Run all is concurrent (up to 3 nodes at once). Stop previously interrupted
    only the most-recent run id and never aborted the client fetches, so other
    in-flight nodes kept running and the requests lingered (a 4s grace timer
    papered over it). Now every in-flight run id is tracked in a set, and Stop
    calls cancelAllRuns([...]) -- which aborts EVERY in-flight run fetch
    (abortInflight) AND interrupts EVERY backend run in the batch
    (cancel_query per id). No request left pending, no engine statement left
    running.
  • The Run-all worker loop now checks the cancel flag before pulling each next
    node, so once you hit Stop no further nodes are launched -- the running node
    and all remaining nodes in the workflow stop.
  • Every run wrapper (preview, run-to-output, chart, validate, browse,
    reconcile, export image, export, export-batch, write-table, read file/
    folder, fetch API, iterator, while) now classifies an abort/cancel via the
    shared isCancelledError and reports "Cancelled" instead of a spurious red
    error. The auto chart-render + validate + directory-list paths clear their
    spinner on cancel instead of flashing "Request aborted".

This is the principle we agreed on, applied to the Nodebook: a Stop (or a
window close, which routes through the same abort) stops all associated
processes -- the running node and the entire rest of the run.

Note on scope: the node runs that go through the flow engine
(run/iterator/while/chart/browse/reconcile/validate) now cancel fully, client
AND server. A few node types call backend ops that aren't interruptible yet
(Profile, Export, Write-table) -- on Stop their client fetch is aborted and the
UI reports cancelled immediately, but the server op may still finish until
parts 2-3 give those a query_id + server-side interrupt. Being explicit about
that rather than implying it's all done.

Tests: a new frontend guard -- Stop wires cancelAllRuns over the full set of
run ids, the worker halts on the cancel flag, and every run catch classifies
cancellation (>=15 guarded catches). The shared-cancel consolidation test now
asserts the Node surface uses the shared module (Stop -> cancelAllRuns) and
classifies via isCancelledError like IDE/Journal. Suite: 410 passed, 0 failed,
15 skipped. tsc clean on the Nodebook (the remaining App.tsx note is the
pre-existing FloatingPanel ambient-stub gap).

build 2026-06-25.249  (v2.4.1)

HDFS fix: "Scan this folder for feeds" stalled on a real tree. /tbsm/output had
hundreds of YYYYMMDD partitions (2017->2020); the scan did a sequential
LISTSTATUS on every date folder (and every feed inside each) -- hundreds-to-
thousands of back-to-back WebHDFS round-trips -- and the request had no timeout,
so the UI spun forever. Reported from the field with a screenshot.

  • Sampled discovery (hdfs.build_feed_index). The feed/file layout is stable
    across date partitions, so the structure is now learned from only the most
    recent `sample` date folders (default 3) -- a handful of LISTSTATUS calls,
    not one per date. Every discovered leaf is then offered across the FULL date
    axis with its path CONSTRUCTED per date (<root>/<YYYYMMDD>/<feed>/<file>, no
    per-date listing). Turns ~O(dates x feeds) round-trips into ~O(sample x
    feeds). sample=0 forces the old exhaustive walk; an explicit dates= set
    still pins both the structure scan and the axis.

  • Load tolerates the gaps. Because paths are now constructed, a date a given
    feed didn't actually produce 404s on OPEN; hdfs_load skips that date (counts
    it as skipped) instead of failing the whole table. Genuine auth/network
    errors still surface. The per-table result reports the dates actually loaded
    plus a skipped count.

  • No more infinite spin. The four HDFS api calls now carry timeouts (connect/
    browse 25s, index 90s, load 600s) so a slow or hung WebHDFS fails cleanly
    with an error instead of hanging the modal.

  • Safer default selection. After a scan the tab now pre-selects only the 3
    newest dates (not all of them -- selecting hundreds would queue hundreds of
    file fetches on Load), with All / None controls and a date count to widen or
    clear quickly.

  • Tests. t_hdfs_feed_index updated for the new semantics (constructed full-
    axis paths) and now asserts the sampling itself (sample=1 discovers
    structure only from the newest date). Suite: 404 passed, 0 failed, 15
    skipped. tsc gate clean in the changed files.

  Reasoned vs tested: the sampling + path construction is unit-tested; the live
  WebHDFS round-trips and the 404-skip during load are reasoned/ported (no
  cluster in the build sandbox). Note: sampling discovers the feed set from
  recent dates -- a feed that existed ONLY in much older, unscanned partitions
  won't appear; raise `sample` or pin an older date= if you need those.

build 2026-06-25.246  (v2.3.3)

HDFS connector — build 1 of N: backend core (browse + feed-first regroup +
multi-date combine). Not yet wired to the UI; endpoints and the React tab
follow in subsequent builds. New module backend/samql_core/hdfs.py.

  • WebHDFSClient — a faithful port of the original desktop tool's HDFS tab:
    plain urllib against the WebHDFS REST API (LISTSTATUS / OPEN), an optional
    user.name query param, NO Kerberos library. That transport is already known
    to work against the target cluster, so it is unchanged. open_stream() now
    accepts offset/length so a future Parquet footer + column-chunk read can be
    done without pulling the whole file. parse_webhdfs_url() normalises
    /webhdfs/v1, explorer.html#..., and bare host[:port] URLs; a HTML reply
    (the NameNode web UI) is detected and explained rather than JSON-parsed.

  • Feed-first regrouping — build_feed_index() pivots the native
    <root>/<date>/<feed>/<file> layout (compact YYYYMMDD date folders) into
    feed -> file -> {date: path}. Non-date dirs (_tmp, archive, bad calendar
    dates) drop out of the date axis; a feed missing on some dates simply has
    fewer dates; an optional dates= window bounds the per-date LISTSTATUS
    fan-out. index_to_tree() flattens it for the UI.

  • Path-minus-date identity — every leaf FILE (not the folder) is its own
    table: table_name() = <root>__<feed>__<file>, each segment sanitised. So
    distinct files in one feed folder stay separate (never auto-unioned), and
    output's / source's look-alike feeds get distinct handles. The date is the
    only axis that collapses.

  • Canonical partition date — the folder 20260601 is parsed into a typed
    DATE '2026-06-01' AS partition_date column by combine_sql(), uniform across
    every feed and independent of whatever date field the CSV itself carries
    (which varies by feed). safe_partition_col() renames the column if it would
    collide with the file's own columns. combine_sql() stacks the selected
    dates with UNION ALL and is path-agnostic (local temp files OR remote URLs),
    so the same SQL serves both the proven "fetch selected dates then read"
    path and a future DuckDB-httpfs direct read. plan_leaf_load() scopes the
    pull to the chosen dates (partition pruning); unselected dates are never
    fetched.

  • Tests — five new backend cases (url+date parsing, feed-first index, naming,
    partition+combine SQL, and the WebHDFS client via an injected fake opener so
    no network is needed). Suite: 400 passed, 0 failed, 15 skipped.

  Reasoned vs tested: all logic above (parsing, regroup, naming, partition,
  SQL generation) is unit-tested. The live WebHDFS HTTP calls and DuckDB
  execution are reasoned/ported (no cluster or duckdb in the build sandbox),
  consistent with how DuckDB paths have always been handled here.

build 2026-06-25.245  (v2.3.2)
*** 2.3.2 -- stability/cleanup pass: unified flow exception handling. ***

A quality + stability tightening pass (no new features), after auditing the
loaders, query path, cancellation, memory release, temp-file cleanup, and node
building for safe consolidations and bottleneck/stall/crash risks.

Change made:
  - Session._flow_exc(e, graph=None) -- every flow handler ended with the same
    two-except body (NodeflowError -> friendly message; engine interrupt ->
    cancelled marker; anything else -> "TypeName: message"). That exact block
    was inlined at 8 handlers; the 7 identical ones now call _flow_exc (the 2
    with handler-specific error text -- the iterator's accumulator hint and the
    table writer's prefix -- were left as-is). Beyond removing duplication this
    GUARANTEES uniform cancellation handling: a handler can no longer
    accidentally omit the interrupt check and mis-report a cancelled run as an
    error. Combined with the earlier _flow_cleanup, each flow handler's teardown
    and error mapping are now single, shared, tested helpers.

Audit findings (checked, deliberately NOT changed -- they're already sound, and
churn here would risk the stability this pass is protecting):
  - Loaders: the CSV/JSON/Parquet/Excel paths are format-specific (each parses
    and registers differently); the progress + LoadCancelled handling is applied
    where each format needs it. No safe shared abstraction without entangling
    formats.
  - Query path: the engine write_lock is the single serialization point by
    design (SQLite is inherently serial; DuckDB serializes its main connection
    for background checkpointing). No redundant locking found; status() and the
    dispatcher stay lock-free.
  - Cancellation: already consolidated (lib/runController on the front end;
    cancel_query interrupts the engine + a cooperative flag on the back end);
    _flow_exc now makes the flow side's cancel-vs-error decision uniform.
  - Memory release: housekeeping already defers the DuckDB checkpoint while a
    run holds the connection (so a reclaim never blocks a query), and
    auto-checkpoint means nothing is lost by deferring.
  - Temp-file cleanup: flow temp tables go through _drop_flow_temps / the shared
    _flow_cleanup on every success and error path; tmputil sweeps stale
    per-instance dirs on startup. The few remaining single DROP TABLE IF EXISTS
    one-liners are clear as-is -- a helper would save nothing and read worse.
  - Node building: the flow handlers share _engine_obj + _materialize_flow +
    _flow_cleanup + _flow_exc; the per-node SQL builders are intentionally
    distinct (pivot/iterator/join differ).

DuckDB paths reasoned as always; SQLite + the change are tested. Backend-only
(no tsc run needed).

Versioning: product 2.3.2 (patch -- refactor); build .245.

Tests: _flow_exc maps NodeflowError -> a flow message (not a cancel) and a
generic exception -> err_str, and the flow handlers route through it.
Suite: 395 passed.

build 2026-06-25.238  (v2.1.2)
*** 2.1.2 -- one shared run/cancel module for the IDE, Journal and Node; fixes
a cancel regression. ***

Consolidation. The three run surfaces had three near-identical copies of the
cancel logic (abort the fetch + interrupt the backend), and they had drifted
apart. They now share one module, lib/runController.ts:
  - cancelOne(queryId, ctrl)   -- abort a run's fetch (when we hold the
    controller) + interrupt the backend for its id. Used by the IDE query
    (run + the two "supersede the previous run" sites), every Journal cell, and
    the Node run.
  - cancelAllRuns(ids)         -- abort EVERY self-owned in-flight request (frees
    the browser connection pool at once, like a reload) + interrupt the backend
    for each id. Used by the Journal "Stop all".
  - isCancelledError(e)        -- the single place that decides whether a thrown
    error is really a cancellation.
Each surface keeps its own run-trigger calls (api.query vs api.nodeflowRun vs
runCell); only the cancel/classify plumbing is shared.

Bug fix (a real one, from 2.0.0). When jsonFetch gained timeouts it began
mapping an aborted fetch to ApiError(0, "Request aborted"). But the IDE and the
Journal still detected a superseded/cancelled run with `e?.name ===
"AbortError"` -- which silently stopped matching, so launching a new query while
one was running, or hitting Stop, surfaced a red "Request aborted" error instead
of quietly cancelling. Both now classify via the shared isCancelledError, so a
cancel reads as a cancel everywhere.

Cancellation guarantees after this pass (verified in the wiring):
  - IDE query: Stop and "supersede on new run" both abort the fetch + interrupt
    the backend; an aborted/superseded run no longer shows an error.
  - Journal: each cell's Stop aborts that cell's fetch + interrupts it; Stop all
    cancels every running cell and frees the pool.
  - Node: Stop interrupts every engine (cancel_query interrupts all engines as a
    safety net, so a folder/iterator/while loop running many statements unwinds
    promptly as cancelled), with a grace-timer UI recovery for a wedged run.
  - Backend: cancel_query interrupts the registered engine AND every engine, and
    sets a cooperative flag the long loops check between statements.

Honest scope: the Node run requests are interrupted on the backend (which
returns "cancelled" promptly) rather than having their fetch aborted client-side
-- doing the latter cleanly needs ~19 run-wrapper catches to treat an abort as a
cancel, which is a focused follow-up; the engine-reset path already frees the
pool for the rare wedged case. No backend behavior changed this round; the work
is the shared module + the regression fix. DuckDB paths reasoned (no DuckDB in
the sandbox); SQLite + the cancel classification are tested.

Versioning: product 2.1.2; build .238.

Tests: a guard that all three surfaces import and use the shared module, that
isCancelledError covers both a raw AbortError and the ApiError(0) mapping, that
cancelAllRuns frees the pool + interrupts the backend, and that the broken
AbortError name-check is gone from the IDE and Journal.

build 2026-06-25.235  (v2.0.0)
*** Product version is now 2.0.0. ***

Fix: the connection-status window + engine reset no longer hang under load (you
had to reload to recover).

Investigation -- the backend was already fine.
- Reset (reset_engines) already orphans the old engine without waiting on its
  lock and rebuilds tables on a BACKGROUND thread, so it returns immediately.
  /api/status is lock-free, and the request dispatcher holds no global lock. So
  nothing server-side blocks the window or the reset behind a busy engine. This
  was NOT already fixed -- the cause was on the client.
- The real cause: the browser allows only a handful of connections per host.
  Under heavy load, requests blocked on the busy engine occupy every slot, and
  jsonFetch had no timeout or abort -- so the status poll and the reset request
  could never complete (they couldn't even get a slot) and hung forever. A full
  page reload was the only recovery because it aborts everything and frees the
  pool.

Fix (client-side).
- jsonFetch now supports a per-request timeout via AbortController and surfaces
  a clear, recoverable error instead of a promise that never settles. The
  status poll is bounded at 8s and the reset at 25s, so neither can hang.
- A standalone abortInflight() aborts all self-owned in-flight requests. The
  reset now calls it FIRST -- the same thing a reload does (free the connection
  pool) -- so the reset request gets a slot and goes through under load instead
  of stalling. Long query/load requests keep their own Stop-based cancellation
  and are left untouched.
- The connection-status window single-flights its poll, so slow polls can't
  stack up and exhaust the pool, and it recovers on its own once slots free.
- Enabling the concurrent-reads flag further reduces the blocking that creates
  the pool pressure in the first place; this fix is the safety net regardless.

Versioning: product version bumped to 2.0.0 (shown in the top bar and
/api/health). The build id keeps incrementing each delivered round (now .235),
and every future change will continue to bump it.

Tests: a frontend guard that jsonFetch carries the timeout/abort plumbing and
maps an abort to a clear error, the status poll and reset are each bounded by a
timeout, abortInflight() exists and frees the pool, and the poll is
single-flighted. Full suite green.
Suite: 376 passed.

Add the test that was missing: proof that a read is actually non-blocking, not

The .233 tests covered the flag, the dispatch logic, the structure (a separate

  early), and the lock uses a generous timeout so it never trips EngineBusy
  during the hold.

build 2026-06-25.233
Add an opt-in flag that lets DuckDB read-only work run on a separate cursor, so
the tables panel / row counts / schema peeks don't queue behind a running build.

What it does (DuckDB only).
- The one real serialization point is the engine: every execute() takes a single
  write_lock, so a row count or tables-panel refresh queues behind a long build
  until it releases. With the flag on, DuckDB's read-only paths -- the catalog
  reconcile (sync_catalog), per-table COUNT(*), and the DESCRIBE schema peek --
  run on a SEPARATE cursor that does NOT take write_lock. That's DuckDB's
  documented one-cursor-per-thread MVCC model and the same primitive the
  streaming export already uses, so those reads proceed while a build holds the
  main connection.
- Every concurrent read falls back to the locked read on any failure (e.g. a
  TEMP table a fresh cursor can't see) -- correctness first. A new dedicated
  catalog lock guards only the in-memory cache reconcile so two refreshes can't
  race it without taking write_lock.
- SQLite is unchanged: one connection, so reads can't run concurrently with a
  write -- that's inherent, and SQLite isn't the large-data engine anyway. The
  whole change is DuckDB-only.

The flag (default OFF, so you can A/B it).
- Off by default. Turn it on three ways: the SAMQL_CONCURRENT_READS=1 env var
  (sets the startup default), POST /api/settings/concurrent-reads {on:true} to
  flip it live without a restart, or Session.set_concurrent_reads(...). The
  current state shows up in /api/status (and the diagnostics view).
- To A/B on the real [.]exe: run a heavy build, refresh the tables panel with the
  flag off (it waits), then again with it on (it shouldn't).

Tests (12 new; 374 total).
- Flag parsing + default-off + runtime toggle + status visibility; SQLite
  read() == execute(); _safe_count routes through read() and falls back to
  execute() on error.
- The REAL DuckDB read() / column_types / sync_catalog concurrent paths are
  exercised by binding the actual methods to a stub connection, so the new
  logic (dispatch, fallback, DESCRIBE mapping, catalog reconcile + drop) is
  tested even though the sandbox has no DuckDB.
- Structure guards (execute_read uses a separate cursor and never acquires
  write_lock; sync_catalog keeps the original locked path when off);
  tables_tree stays correct as the flag toggles; an HTTP toggle test; and a
  real-DuckDB functional check that's dormant here but runs on your build.
Note: the sandbox has no DuckDB, so the actual concurrency is reasoned about
(on the proven export-cursor primitive + MVCC) and the real-DuckDB test in the
suite will exercise it on your machine. Default OFF means nothing changes until
you flip it.
Suite: 374 passed.

  couldn't touch it; it would run to completion or the 60s timeout. Now the

  between pages, and a streaming download to a temp file stops between chunks.
  A single in-flight request is still bounded by the 60s timeout (a socket
  mid-read isn't interrupted), but Stop no longer waits on a multi-page or
  large-file fetch. The node reports "cancelled" rather than an error, and the

  them by pulling every row of every file back through Python (it materialized
  each file's whole table in memory, rebuilt a dict + tuple per row, then
  re-inserted them). For a folder of large files that's millions of Python
  objects -- very slow, memory-heavy enough to swap, and with no progress, so
  it looked frozen on "Reading folder…".

  which stacks them inside the engine and aligns columns by name (missing ->
  NULL) exactly as before -- no row-by-row Python round-trip. If the columns or
  types don't line up for a native stack it falls back to the previous Python
  union, so nothing that loaded before stops loading. SQLite (which can't read
  files and has no BY NAME) keeps the Python path; folders targeting SQLite are
  small.
- The folder read was not re-firing in a loop and was not hung -- it was the
  slow combine. A folder of large files should now finish in a fraction of the
  time.

Tests: paginated fetch aborts between pages on cancel; a streaming download
aborts mid-stream; load_api returns a cancelled result; an API node fetch
reports cancelled and clears its run flag; the UI passes the run id through the
API fetch (and iterator / while / folder / directory). The folder union-by-name
behaviour stays covered.

build 2026-06-25.223
Fix: whole numbers entered in a grid (or coming from JSON) are now stored as
numbers, not text -- so a formula that does arithmetic on them works on DuckDB.
A column like col1 holding whole numbers used to be typed as text unless its
NAME looked like a measure (amount, qty, total, ...). On SQLite that's harmless
(it coerces text to a number on the fly), but DuckDB is strict: col1 + 1 over a
text column raises "BinderException: No function matches the given name and
argument types '(VARCHAR, INTEGER_LITERAL)'". That bind failure also left a
downstream node's column picker empty (the probe couldn't compile the upstream
formula), which looked like the node "wasn't updating / pulling previous data"
and showed +0 columns.
- Type inference now treats values that arrive as real numbers -- a grid cell
  already coerced to int/float, or a JSON number -- as numeric no matter what
  the column is called; a number is a number. The name-based "this might be an
  identifier" heuristic still applies to *string* digit-runs from CSV, so
  account numbers and zip codes with leading zeros stay text exactly as before.
- Result: a createtable / JSON column of whole numbers becomes BIGINT (DOUBLE
  if any value is fractional), so col1 + 1 binds and runs on DuckDB, the
  upstream compiles, and the downstream node's columns populate again.
- Tests: native int / float under any column name -> numeric; mixed, boolean,
  and over-wide integers stay text; CSV string digit-runs unchanged (generic
  name stays text, a measure name -> numeric, a leading zero stays text); a
  grid table of whole numbers creates numeric columns and col1 + 1 computes.
Note on the other case: a column that is genuinely text (e.g. a CSV column of
digit-strings you want to sum) still needs an explicit cast -- CAST(col AS
BIGINT) + 1, or a Parse / cast node -- because DuckDB won't coerce text inside
arithmetic. The strict-engine binder error itself can't be exercised by the
in-repo tests (no DuckDB here); the typing that prevents it is verified on
SQLite. Suite: 346 passed.

build 2026-06-25.222
Observability + recovery for silent hangs. When the app stalls with nothing in
the terminal, that's a blocked call, not a crash -- this build makes the block
visible and gives you ways out, without ever cancelling a healthy long load.
- Stall watchdog: a background thread watches in-flight operations and, when
  one stops making progress, writes every thread's stack to a log
  (stall_watchdog.log in the instance temp dir) so the stuck call is named. It
  is progress-based, not time-based -- a load that keeps flushing batches (even
  for many minutes) keeps a fresh heartbeat and is never flagged -- and it is
  observe-only: it never cancels or interrupts anything.
- Heartbeats everywhere: loads (both engines), result/export streaming, and
  queries / flow runs all stamp progress as they go, so the dashboard and the
  watchdog see accurate liveness for every long operation.
- Activity & connections dashboard (Settings -> Activity & connections): a live
  panel (GET /api/status) showing in-flight operations with rows processed and
  time since last progress, which engine connections are busy, the background
  thread count, the restore state, and the last stall. An operation idle 20s+
  is flagged so a genuine hang stands out from a slow-but-progressing one.
- Reset engines: one-click recovery (POST /api/engine/reset) that swaps in
  fresh engines and rebuilds your loaded tables from the manifest without
  restarting the app. It never waits on a wedged engine's lock (it orphans the
  old one); anything not saved to a file is cleared, and a table whose source
  moved is skipped (exactly as a restart would).
- Interrupt-aware cancel: cancel now reaches engine.interrupt(), so a stuck
  single statement can be broken mid-call, not only between batches.
- Restore yields to you: session restore defers to your first load/query/run
  instead of holding the engine lock ahead of it (bounded so a long user op
  can't starve restore).
- Bounded DuckDB connect: opening the on-disk DuckDB file is time-bounded
  (15s); a wedged or locked path falls back to in-memory instead of hanging on
  first use.
- get_duckdb is synchronized: concurrent first-ops build exactly one DuckDB
  manager, with no racing second connection or temp file.
Note: the DuckDB-specific paths (interrupting a stuck execute, the bounded
connect, the DuckDB side of reset) can't be exercised by the in-repo tests,
which have no DuckDB. The registry, watchdog, /api/status, reset rebuild,
cancel wiring, restore-yield, connect timeout, and get_duckdb sync are all
covered here; confirm the DuckDB-only behaviour on the real machine.
Suite: 344 passed.

build 2026-06-25.221

Stall / "failed to fetch" cascade -- audit + hardening
-------------------------------------------------------
Full review of how a stuck or failed SQLite/DuckDB operation impacts later
loads and table-creations, plus fixes so one wedged operation can no longer
take the whole app down.

* Deadline-bounded engine lock. Every engine touches its connection under a
  single write lock. Previously a foreground operation (create-table, load,
  query, export) would wait on that lock FOREVER if another operation was
  stuck -- a wedged on-disk DuckDB call, a slow checkpoint, or the startup
  restore replaying earlier loads. The waiting worker threads piled up and
  never returned, which the UI surfaced as a frozen spinner and then the
  opaque "failed to fetch". The connection lock is now deadline-bounded: a
  foreground op waits at most ~30s for the engine and then fails fast with a
  clear, retryable "engine is busy / may be stuck -- retry or restart"
  message instead of hanging. This bounds only the WAIT to acquire the lock,
  never a running operation -- a legitimately long load/query that already
  holds the lock still runs to completion; only operations queued behind it
  are bounded. Re-entrancy and the non-blocking acquire used by the
  background checkpoint are preserved.

* Malformed / oversized uploads no longer drop the connection. The
  multipart/form-data parse ran outside the request handler's error guard,
  so a bad upload body could close the socket with no response -- another
  source of "failed to fetch" when loading data. It now returns a clean
  HTTP 400 and the server stays responsive.

Net effect: a failed or stuck load/query can no longer cascade into
indefinitely-stalled table creations and loads. Worst case is now a prompt,
clear error rather than a hang. (Note: the underlying cause of a DuckDB call
wedging on a slow/locked on-disk path is environmental and can't be
reproduced here -- this change prevents the cascade and the dead-app state
it caused.)
----------------------------------------------------------------
build 2026-06-25.220
Fixes for two DuckDB-specific stalls reported from the Windows build:

- Background maintenance checkpoint no longer blocks a run. The periodic
  DuckDB CHECKPOINT (which flushes the on-disk WAL) holds the connection
  lock; on a slow or networked path it could make the very next flow run
  sit on "Running <table>…". It now yields -- it is skipped while a query
  or flow run is in flight (and rescheduled for the next idle moment) and
  never waits for the connection lock (non-blocking acquire), so it can no
  longer queue behind a query and then seize the connection the instant it
  is freed. DuckDB auto-checkpoints the WAL regardless, so nothing is lost.

- Cancelling a Nodebook run no longer requires a page refresh. If an
  interrupted run does not return promptly, the editor now recovers the UI
  to idle after a short grace period instead of stranding it on
  "Cancelling…"; a late straggler result is absorbed so it cannot desync a
  subsequent run.

build 2026-06-25.203
Tableau / Power BI export now writes Parquet, and the option shows up in both
the results Export menu and the Output node's file type.
- Was CSV, now Parquet. Both Tableau and Power BI open Parquet natively -- it
  is typed, columnar, and the closest openly-writable format to Tableau's
  .hyper extract. Real .hyper (Tableau) and .pbix (Power BI) are proprietary
  binaries that need each vendor's SDK; bundling those would break the
  stdlib-only, no-extra-dependency design that keeps the backend auditable, so
  SamQL can't write them. Parquet is the practical, lossless interchange both
  tools import directly. (Needs pyarrow, which is present on this machine.)

  "Tableau (.parquet)" and "Power BI (.parquet)" (relabeled from the old, and
  misleading, "(CSV)"), alongside CSV / JSON / NDJSON / Excel / Parquet -- all
  the Parquet-based ones gated behind pyarrow. The Output node's Format list
  gained Parquet plus the same Tableau / Power BI entries (each writes a
  .parquet file). The single-file writer, the batch "Run all" writer, and the

build 2026-06-25.202
Iterator fixes from a screenshot: the cryptic "$" error, the perceived
column-name desync, and the table name clearing after a run.
- Clear error instead of `unrecognized token: "$"`. When an iterator's loop
  body references a ${name} the values row doesn't provide, the ${name}
  survived substitution and a lone $ reached SQL, so every pass failed with an
  opaque engine error. The iterator now checks up front and returns one clear
  message naming the unbound variable and listing the fields the values row
  actually provides (e.g. "references ${nope}, but the values row has no such
  field. Available: col1, col2 ..."). That is the real cause of what looked
  like "column names aren't syncing": a formula/SQL ${name} that doesn't match
  a column of the wired values table.
- Column names do sync. Verified against the live engine: a Create-table node
  with columns col1/col2 outputs col1/col2. The dog1/dog2 seen in the grid came
  from a row of values being treated as a header row (pasting "dog<TAB>dog" as
  the first line makes those the column names, de-duplicated to dog1/dog2). The
  underlying problem was the name mismatch above, now surfaced plainly.
- The table name no longer clears after a run. The iterator and while-loop run
  handlers wrote `table: <result>` unconditionally; a run that wrote nothing
  (e.g. the failed pass above) returns no table, which blanked the accumulator
  name and blocked a simple rerun. They now keep the existing name when a run
  produced none, so you can correct the formula and run again -- overwriting or
  appending per the node's reset/accumulate setting.
- Tests added for all three. Suite: 299.

build 2026-06-25.200
Final performance + memory pass before shipping.
- That "slower" text was only a startup note: "loading data engine (first
  launch is slower)" -- it meant the first launch takes a couple seconds to
  load the data engine (DuckDB) and warm caches, not that the running server is
  slow. Reworded to "loading data engine - first start takes a few seconds" so
  it's clearly about startup, not runtime.
- Lower request latency: the HTTP handler now disables Nagle's algorithm
  (TCP_NODELAY). The UI makes many tiny calls (progress polls, column batches,
  run status); on a loopback connection Nagle only added coalescing delay, so
  sending small packets immediately keeps every interaction snappy.
- Audited and confirmed the rest is already tuned for speed and bounded memory:
  DuckDB runs multi-threaded (cores-1, capped), with a machine-sized memory cap
  that spills to a temp dir, the object cache on, and insertion-order
  bookkeeping off; SQLite uses its fast PRAGMAs (memory journal, mmap, big
  cache); JSON uses orjson when present; large responses gzip; query results are
  parquet-backed (compact, spillable) with LRU eviction that never drops the
  newest; client-abort console noise stays suppressed.
- A new guard test locks all of the above in so a later edit can't quietly
  regress the performance or memory wiring. Suite: 296.

build 2026-06-25.194
Quiet the harmless ConnectionAbortedError ([WinError 10053]) tracebacks the
backend console spammed.
- What they were: the browser cancels in-flight requests all the time and
  harmlessly -- when you navigate, supersede a running query, or stop polling a
  progress endpoint while its reply is still being written. The work already
  finished server-side; only delivering the response failed, so the socket write
  raised a ConnectionError that there's nothing to act on. The default server
  printed a full traceback for each one, which looked alarming and buried real
  errors.
- Fix: the server now swallows that "client went away mid-write" family
  (ConnectionError: WinError 10053 / ECONNRESET / broken pipe) with no console
  output, while every other error still prints as before so genuine bugs surface.
- Not a functional bug: no request was lost and nothing crashed -- the client
  had simply stopped listening. This only removes the noise.
- Test: drives the real server's handle_error -- a client-abort is silent, a
  genuine error still prints. Suite: 289.

build 2026-06-25.193
Three connected iterator-container bugs from a screenshot review.
- "Name the loop variable" on Run. A container iterator is driven by the table
  wired to its top "values" port (each row is one pass, its columns bound as
  ${vars}) and uses no loop-variable name -- but Run still demanded one and
  bailed, so the iterator never actually ran. Removed that stale gate; the
  backend already accepts a wired values table (and still reports a clear error
  if neither a values table nor a classic driver is set).

  above: because Run bailed, the accumulator table was never built, so
  previewing the out port (which reads that table) failed. With Run working the
  table is created and the out port reads it normally.

  are empty when only the values port is wired. It now lists the accumulator
  TABLE's own columns -- the keys the idempotent re-run matches on must exist
  there -- with a hint to run once first when the table doesn't exist yet.
- Tests: a backend run of a container iterator off a wired values table with no
  loop variable (binds ${vars} per pass, accumulates, out port reads it), plus a
  frontend structural guard. Suite: 288.
Heads-up: a container body that reads data (e.g. Summarize) needs the side "in"
port wired with the rows it processes each pass -- the values port supplies the
per-pass ${vars}, the "in" port supplies the data.

build 2026-06-24.180
Iterator: a top "values" connector to drive the loop from a wired table.

  The iterator node now has TWO inputs:
    * a new connector on the TOP edge ("values") that takes a table whose
      rows drive the loop -- one pass per row, each row's columns bound as
      scalar ${vars}; and
    * the existing body / side input on the LEFT ("in").

  Wiring a table into the top input overrides the configured driver (list /
  date-range / column / rows), which stays as the fallback when nothing is
  wired -- so existing iterators are unchanged. This works whether the
  iterator runs an upstream body (classic) or holds inner children (container
  mode, where the left input is the optional side feed).

  Why: previously the only way to feed an iterator a set of values was the
  inspector's driver config; you couldn't just wire the table that produces
  them. The top connector makes that direct.

  Implementation: a small "top input" concept in the canvas (the renderer and
  the wire-anchor geometry agree on which ports sit on the top edge vs the
  left), plus the backend loop reading the wired "vars" input via the same
  row-materialiser the container model already used.

build 2026-06-24.177
New: "Query the file in place" load mode (no copy).

  The load dialog's file tab now has a "How to load" choice:
    * Copy into a table (default) -- today's behaviour, materialises the file.
    * Query the file in place -- creates a DuckDB view over the file via the
      native read_csv_auto / read_json_auto / read_parquet readers, so nothing
      is copied into storage. The "load" is instant and memory stays low; the
      file is read on each query.

  When to use it: Parquet is the sweet spot -- queries push column + row-group
  filters down into the file, so it's fast AND cheap. A CSV works too but is
  re-parsed on every query, so for repeated querying convert hot CSVs to
  Parquet (a transparent CSV->Parquet cache is the planned follow-on). The
  view's source path must persist, so this is wired to the path-based load
  (your real file on disk), not the drag-and-drop upload (whose temp copy is
  deleted after loading).

  Safe fallback: if DuckDB isn't available, or the file is Excel, view mode
  quietly falls back to a normal materialised load rather than failing.

  Tests: 269 passed (was 267). New t_load_view_mode drives the view path (via a
  faked DuckDB) and the no-DuckDB materialise fallback live; t_load_view_mode_
  wiring pins the view SQL and the mode plumbing across loader -> session ->
  server -> api -> dialog.

  Up next: UI updates.

  Verified live in sandbox: the mode plumbing end-to-end and the fallback (no
  DuckDB here). Unverified (no real DuckDB in the sandbox): the actual
  CREATE VIEW ... read_*() and querying it on your machine -- please give it a
  try (Parquet first) and tell me how it feels.

build 2026-06-24.176
Fix: "Flatten JSON" now works on API-loaded tables (no source file needed).

  Flattening a DuckDB table into relational tables used to require the original
  JSON file on disk. A table loaded straight from the API connector has no such
  file -- the streamed response is spooled to a temp file and deleted right
  after loading -- so flatten failed with "No source file on disk for '<table>'".

  flatten_json now falls back to dumping the DuckDB table itself to a temporary
  JSON file (COPY ... TO (FORMAT JSON) -- nested STRUCT/LIST columns are written
  back out as nested JSON) and flattens that. So flatten works for any DuckDB
  JSON table, file-backed or not; the flattened relational tables still land in
  SQLite. The temp dump is removed afterward.

  Tests: 267 passed (was 266). New t_flatten_no_source_dumps drives the no-file
  path end-to-end with an injected DuckDB whose COPY writes NDJSON, asserting the
  root + nested child tables come out in SQLite.

  Next (separate build): the "load / query the file in place" option in the load
  dialog -- it's a new DuckDB view mode plus a dialog toggle, and since I can't
  run DuckDB in the sandbox I'm shipping it on its own so you can verify the
  view behaviour cleanly without it being tangled up with this fix.

  Verified live in sandbox: the dump->JSON->flatten->SQLite path (via a fake
  DuckDB) and the full suite. Unverified (no real DuckDB here): the actual
  DuckDB COPY ... TO (FORMAT JSON) on your machine -- the JSON reader already
  tolerates array / NDJSON / concatenated output, so any of those will load.

build 2026-06-24.169
Fix + audit: nodes now reliably show the columns coming from their connected
inputs. The filter node in particular wasn't showing them at all.

The inspector fetches a selected node's upstream columns to fill its column
pickers -- a formula's [Field] suggestions, a join's left/right key dropdowns, a
filter's condition fields, a summarize's group-by, and so on. The list of which
input ports to fetch for each node type was hand-maintained, and it had drifted:
the filter node was missing from it, so a filter's dropdowns stayed empty. And
because a filter often sits upstream of a formula or a join, a filter you
couldn't configure broke the chain feeding them -- which is the most likely
reason the formula and join nodes looked broken too.

The fetch now derives the wanted ports straight from each node's own port
definition (PORTS[type].inputs) instead of a separate list. So every
input-bearing node is covered automatically, the fetched column keys always
match what each inspector reads, and no future node can be missed.

Full audit. I cross-checked every node type: for each inspector that reads input
columns, the column keys it reads (in / left / right / in1..in5) all correspond
to that node's declared input ports, and all are now fetched. Only the filter
node was actually broken; formula, join, reconcile, anti-join, multi-join,
summarize, sort and the rest were already wired correctly. A new test encodes
this audit permanently: it fails if any inspector reads a column key with no
matching input port, or if the fetch ever stops deriving from the port table.

Tests: the new audit test plus the existing suite. Suite: 260 passed.

Verified live on the stdlib SQLite engine: column resolution for single-input,
two-input and multi-input node shapes returns the right columns. The audit test
is static (it reads the UI source). Not exercised in this sandbox: the dropdowns
actually filling in a browser. If a formula or join still shows no input columns
after this build, that points to a different cause (e.g. the upstream node can't
resolve its columns) -- send a screenshot and I'll trace it.

build 2026-06-24.167
New (engine): the iterator can now be a CONTAINER that loops a mini-pipeline,
the way you asked for. This build lands the backend engine; the canvas UI (the
top-edge variables port and drag-and-drop inner steps) is the next build, so the
new mode isn't reachable from the app yet -- it is exercised here by tests.

How the new model works. An iterator that holds inner children (a group-style
mini-pipeline) runs those children once per ROW of a wired "variables" input.
Each row's columns are bound as scalar ${vars}. An optional side input feeds the
inner pipeline's first step; some loops don't need it (they hit an API or read a
file per row instead). Every pass's output is appended -- or reduced -- into one
accumulator table, exactly like the existing iterator.

The part you were worried about -- API and file-browser nodes inside the loop.
Those nodes take no data input, but the row's scalar variables still reach them,
because each pass deep-substitutes ${var} into every string in every nested node
config: a child API node's URL / query params / headers, and a file-browser's
glob. So https://service/${region}/data becomes .../US/data on the US pass, and
/data/*_${as_of}.csv becomes /data/*_20260101.csv. API children are fetched
fresh each pass against the substituted URL; the file-browser's glob compiles
straight to DuckDB with the substituted path. Verified end to end below.

Variables source. The rows come from the wired "variables" input (read once;
optional distinct). If that input isn't wired, the iterator falls back to the
existing list / column / date-range / rows drivers, so nothing that works today
stops working.

Back-compatible. An iterator with no inner children runs through the original
code path untouched -- driver plus an upstream wired body -- so existing
iterators behave exactly as before. The container path is taken only when inner
children are present.

Tests: a new backend test drives a real container loop on SQLite (side data
filtered by ${region} and tagged by a formula, two passes, four rows
accumulated), proves a nested API node receives the per-row substituted URL

the classic driver+body iterator still runs. Suite: 258 passed.

build 2026-06-24.166
Fix: a step inside a group can now see the columns of every input it is wired
to, not just its first one.

A group lets a step (for example a join) draw its inputs from the group's own
input ports via "Step inputs". The backend already fed those bindings correctly,
but the inspector only ever fetched column names for the step's FIRST input port
(the step above it). So a join inside a group showed its left-key dropdown
populated and its right-key dropdown empty -- you had wired and bound the second
input, yet could not pick a key from it.

The inspector now resolves EACH input port the same way the group itself does: a
port bound to one of the group's inputs reads that input's columns; the first
port otherwise reads the step above it (or the group's primary input for the
first step); an unbound extra port stays empty, as it should, because nothing
feeds it. So a join, multi-join, or any multi-input step inside a group now
offers keys from both sides.

This is the same inspector that got the no-flicker fix last build, so both
behaviours -- steady column lists while typing, and full column access for group
steps -- now hold everywhere, top-level nodes and group children alike.

Tests: the group multi-input test now also asserts the column endpoint returns
each bound port's columns (left from group input 1, right from group input 2),
and a wiring check covers the inspector resolving both bound and step-above
ports. Suite: 257 passed.

Verified live on the stdlib SQLite engine (the group's bound join resolves and
the per-port column lookup returns each side's columns). The Vite production
build and the visual dropdowns remain unverified in this sandbox (no browser);
the React change passes the esbuild bundle and the curated tsc type-check.

build 2026-06-24.165
Fix: typing in an inspector field no longer makes the column lists flicker.

The inspector fetches a node's upstream column names to populate its column
pickers -- a Select's fields, an Iterator's replace-keys and reduce columns, a
join's keys, and so on. That fetch cleared the cached columns to empty at the
top of its effect AND re-ran on every change to the graph, so each keystroke in
any field (typing the Iterator's list of values, or a column's rename) blanked
every column-derived list for an instant and then refilled it as the refetch
returned -- a visible flicker.

Now the cached columns are cleared only when the SELECTED node changes (so a
freshly selected node still never shows the previous node's columns), and the
fetch effect no longer blanks them while you edit the current node. The lists
stay put and only update in place if the upstream columns actually change. The
fix is shared by every inspector, so the Select "configure columns" list, the
Iterator's replace-keys / reduce checkboxes, and the rest are all steady while
typing.

Tests: a wiring check pins the behaviour -- the input columns are cleared on a
dedicated [selId] effect, and the old blank-at-the-top-of-the-fetch pattern is
gone. Suite: 257 passed.

The flicker was a render-timing issue only observable in a browser; the fix is
verified by the structural check plus the esbuild bundle and curated tsc, but
the visual result itself can't be exercised in this sandbox (no browser).

build 2026-06-24.164
Change: the filter node's custom logic (and the formula node's expressions) are
bare expressions -- you write just the condition or formula, never a SELECT
wrapper -- and a spreadsheet-style IF() now works on both engines.

The filter's "write custom filter logic" box already accepted a bare boolean
expression (it is wrapped into the WHERE for you) with [Field] references and a
function palette; comparisons, CASE, IN, BETWEEN, AND/OR and functions like
UPPER all worked with no SELECT. What did NOT work was IF(cond, then, else):
SQLite has no IF() function, so it errored there while working on DuckDB. IF(...)
is now rewritten to a portable CASE WHEN cond THEN then ELSE else END before
compiling, so the conditional works on either engine. The same rewrite is shared
by the formula node (whose placeholder advertised IF), so IF works there too.
Nesting, [Field] references inside the arguments, and commas / parentheses
inside string literals are all handled; a malformed IF (not exactly three
arguments) is passed through so the engine reports a clear error; and IF is
matched only as a standalone call, so a column or word ending in "if" is left
alone. Every other function (UPPER, COALESCE, regexp_*, CASE, IN, BETWEEN, ...)
already passed straight through and still does -- regexp_* are registered on
SQLite to match DuckDB.

IF was added to the function palette next to CASE WHEN, so the conditional is
one click to insert.

Tests: +1 -- the IF -> CASE rewrite is unit-tested for nesting, string-literal
and word-boundary safety, and three-argument-only passthrough; plus end-to-end
IF in both a filter condition and a formula on the SQLite engine, and a bare

covers the palette entry and the shared expression prep. Suite: 257 passed.

field reorders it, and its keep / type / rename (the output column header)

emits the columns in that order and every downstream node reads them in that
order.

To make a reorder stick, the field-sync that keeps a Select aligned with its
upstream columns now PRESERVES the order you set: surviving columns stay where
you put them, a newly-arriving column (a formula's new column, or a column an

build 2026-06-24.161
New: a reduce/fold accumulator mode for the iterator, and a Repeat-until
controller node.

Iterator -- reduce mode. Alongside append and replace-keys, the iterator's
accumulator can now FOLD each pass into one row per key with a distributive
aggregation (sum/min/max/count). After each pass the accumulator is collapsed by
the key columns, so it never grows past the number of distinct keys -- the point
of a chunked map-reduce: iterate over chunks, aggregate each chunk in the body,
and fold the partials into a grand total. Only distributive aggregations are
offered; fold averages as sum and count yourself (distinct-counts cannot be
folded across chunks at all). Configured by an "Accumulate" dropdown plus key
columns and per-measure aggregations in the iterator inspector.

Repeat-until controller (the "while" node). A new loop controller that repeats
its wired body until a pass adds no new rows to the accumulator (a fixpoint) or
an iteration cap is hit. Each iteration re-resolves the graph -- so the body can
read the very table it is building and compute the next batch -- and appends
through the same append / replace-key / reduce machinery the iterator uses. The
1-based iteration number binds to an optional loop variable (${i}). For a clean
fixpoint the body should return only new rows (e.g. an antijoin against the
accumulator) or use replace-keys; a body that reads the accumulator should seed
it first and turn "clear before first pass" off. Like the iterator it writes to
a named table rather than exposing a data port -- read the result with an Input
node. New backend endpoint /api/while/run.

Fix: the flow cache is now cleared at the top of each controller iteration. The
cache keys on graph text, which is identical every iteration, so a body that
read the accumulator it was growing could be handed a stale earlier result and
the loop could converge one round too early. Iterations now always recompute
against the latest rows.

Tests: +2 (the iterator reduce mode folds partial sums by key and rejects a
non-distributive fn; the controller computes a transitive closure to a fixpoint
and stops a non-converging body at its cap). Port-parity and feature-wiring
checks were extended to cover the new node and endpoint. Suite: 255 passed.

Verified live on the stdlib SQLite engine (reduce folds 100+50=150 for one
region; the closure converges to its 6 pairs at iteration 3; a runaway body
stops at the cap with a note). DuckDB, the Vite production build and the visual
inspector remain unverified in this sandbox (no DuckDB, no browser) -- the
React/CSS changes pass the esbuild bundle and the curated tsc type-check.

build 2026-06-24.158
api: retry + rate-limit (exponential backoff)

The API node can retry transient failures instead of giving up on the first one.
A new "Retries on 429 / 5xx" setting (0 = off, the default) controls it:

- Retries an HTTP 408 / 425 / 429 (rate-limited) / 500 / 502 / 503 / 504 and
  network-level errors (timeout / connection reset / DNS) with full-jitter
  exponential backoff (base 0.5s, capped at 30s).
- After the retries are exhausted on a retryable status the result becomes a
  clear error ("HTTP 503 after N attempt(s); gave up retrying") rather than
  letting an error body load as if it were data.
- Works on every fetch path: each page of a paginated pull is retried
  independently, and the streaming spool-to-disk path retries too (the
  destination is re-truncated on each attempt).
- Composes with the rest: a give-up can still be routed to the errors output
  when Continue on error is on, and an iterator retries within each pass.

Mechanics (apiload): _retry_plan normalizes {retries, base_delay, max_delay};
_backoff_delay does full-jitter exponential backoff; _is_transient classifies a
status/error; _fetch_with_retries and _spool_with_retries wrap the fetch and
spool seams. fetch_all_pages and load_api take retry= and an injectable sleep=;
the session passes cfg["retry"] and an injectable _api_sleep, so backoff is
testable without real waiting.

Tests: +2 backend -- the retry runner recovers after 503s, gives up with an
error, never retries a 404, retries network errors, honors retries=0, and keeps
backoff within [0, cap]; wired through the node it recovers a 503->200 fetch,
exhausts retries under continuous 503 + continue-on-error, and retries the
streaming spool path. Suite: 249 passed / 0 failed / 12 skipped.

Note: backoff is purely exponential; a server's Retry-After header is not yet
honored (the fetch seam doesn't surface response headers -- a follow-up).
Validated with injected fetch/spool + injected sleep (no network, no real
delays).

build 2026-06-24.157
api: error-output port (continue-on-error)

The API node gained a second output, errors, and a Continue on error toggle:

- With the toggle off (default) a failed fetch is a hard error, exactly as
  before.
- With it on, a failed fetch no longer stops the run: the status, message and
  URL are written to the node's errors output (a small fixed-schema table --
  ok, status, error, url) and the data (out) output is left empty. Wire errors
  to a write node to persist failures, or preview them from the inspector.
- The errors table always exists after a fetch with a stable schema (0 rows on
  success, 1 row on a captured failure), so anything wired to it keeps working
  whether or not the latest fetch failed. It is created in the same engine as
  the data (the default engine on a failure), so out and errors never straddle
  engines.

Mechanics: NODE_PORTS / PORTS for apinode now expose out + err; node_output_sql
serves the error table on the err port; fetch_api_node reads continue_on_error,
builds the error table via the engines' shared add_table_streaming, and returns
{fetched:false, err_table, err_rows} instead of {error} on a soft failure; the
node's hidden-table cache tracks both tables and drops both on re-fetch;
_flow_engine_target pins on the data or the error table. Frontend: the errors
port renders (labelled "errors"), a Continue on error checkbox, a
captured-errors readout + Preview errors button, and doFetchApi handles the
soft-fail return.

Tests: +1 backend -- success gives a 0-row err table and a 2-row out; a 503 with
continue-on-error captures one error row (error + status columns present), the
out port errors with no data, and continue-off stays a hard error. The
port-parity guard (frontend/backend port sets match) and the updated wiring
check both pass. Suite: 247 passed / 0 failed / 12 skipped.

build 2026-06-24.156
api: stream large responses to disk (memory safety)

The API node's common single-response fetch no longer reads the whole HTTP body
into memory. It spools the response to a temp file in bounded chunks and loads
from disk:

- DuckDB reads the spooled file directly (read_json_auto) with no Python parse
  at all -- the big win for large payloads and the usual no-records-path case.
- SQLite parses records from the file via the shared streaming reader (ijson
  when installed, stdlib otherwise); the flattener still buffers the flattened
  rows, but the raw-bytes + decoded-text + parsed-objects tripling is gone.
- A hard byte cap is enforced while spooling (512 MB default): an oversize
  response stops at the cap and returns a clear "fetch a smaller payload" error
  instead of exhausting memory.

The in-memory path is unchanged for the two cases that need it: an injected
fetcher (tests and the iterator, which already hold parsed data) and multi-page
pagination (which concatenates pages and is bounded by max_pages). A new spool=
seam mirrors the fetch= seam, so the spool-to-disk pipeline is fully testable
without a network.

New internals in apiload: spool_response (chunked copy + cap), fetch_to_file
(streaming HTTP -> file), _records_from_file (bounded record stream reusing the
existing stream_json_records), _api_duckdb_file (DuckDB reads the file), and a
shared _load_records. session gained an injectable _api_spooler.

Tests: +3 backend -- the chunked spool writes verbatim and enforces the cap;
records stream from a spooled file (top-level array, nested json_path, lone
object); and the end-to-end streaming fetch (injected spooler, no network)
parses from disk into a table, resolves ${vars} before spooling, handles a
nested records-path, and surfaces a spooler error. Suite: 246 passed / 0 failed
/ 12 skipped.

A bug caught mid-build by the suite: the flattener takes a list, not a generator
(it treats a non-list as one record), so streamed records are materialised
before loading -- fine, since the flattener buffers anyway. Validated by the
spool + parse-from-disk tests on SQLite; the DuckDB direct-file read and a real
network transfer weren't exercised here (no DuckDB, no network), though both
degrade gracefully to the tested paths.

build 2026-06-24.155
flow: Iterator node -- loop a driver, accumulate into one table

THE iterator. A new Iterator node repeats a body once per value and appends
every result into a single table, keeping the graph acyclic (the body feeds the
iterator's input; the loop runs inside the node).

- Loop variable: name it (e.g. as_of) and the body uses ${as_of}. Each pass the
  graph is re-resolved with the variable set to the current value.
- Drivers (where the values come from): a list you type (one per line); the

  month step, month clamps the day).

  in the path, or -- the headline -- an API node whose URL/params use ${var}.
  The iterator re-fetches each API node in the body per pass, so a
  ${region}/${as_of}-driven endpoint is called once per value and the responses
  stack into the accumulator.
- Accumulator: appends into a named table (reusing the by-name / idempotent
  write from .152). "Clear before the first pass" resets it; choosing key
  columns makes re-runs idempotent (delete-then-insert) instead of doubling.

  value (recording it) instead of aborting -- the toast reports e.g. "7/9
  passes, 2 failed". Per-pass temp tables are dropped as it goes.
- The accumulator is a normal table; point an Input node at it to use the
  combined result downstream. Run all runs the iterator too.

used by both the write node and the iterator (behaviour unchanged; the .152

output: write-node append / overwrite + idempotent re-runs

  replace a same-named table) or Append (add the incoming rows, creating the
