  inserting, any rows already in the table whose keys match the incoming data
  are deleted first -- so re-running (or re-pulling a day) replaces those rows
  instead of duplicating them. The target table name also honours ${variables}
  now (e.g. tx_${region}).

This is the accumulator the iterator will append into on each pass.

Tests: +1 backend test (overwrite resets; append grows; idempotent re-append by
key doesn't duplicate; a bad key is reported) and +1 UI wiring check (the mode
select + replace-key picker, front and back). Suite: 237 passed / 0 failed / 12

build 2026-06-24.151
variable node + ${name} substitution (foundation for the iterator)

- New Variable node: define name -> value pairs in its config, then reference
  them anywhere in the workflow as ${name}. Quote it for a string literal
  ('${as_of}'), leave it bare for a number or identifier (${n}). It lives in the
  Create palette group, has no ports (a definition node, like a Text note), and
  shows its current values on the canvas.
- ${name} tokens are resolved once, up front, as a pure graph -> graph pass
  before any SQL is compiled -- so they work in SQL nodes, filter conditions,
  formulas, and every other text field, with no change to the compilation path.
  Unknown tokens are left untouched (a typo surfaces instead of vanishing), and
  the Variable node's own config is never rewritten (no chaining / cycles).
- Built to be driven by the upcoming iterator: the resolver takes an optional
  per-pass override context, so the iterator can rebind a variable each
  iteration without touching anything else.

This is step 1 of the iterator / dynamic-file / dynamic-API plan; the
substitution engine is the shared foundation the dynamic nodes and the iterator
all build on.

build 2026-06-20.143
incremental flow execution (hardening + tests)

The Nodebook already had a content-addressed flow cache: each boundary
node's output is fingerprinted over its config + input subtree + data
epoch + engine, materialised to a __nbcache_* temp table, and reused on
re-run instead of recomputed. Editing a node changes its fingerprint
(and every node downstream), so only those recompute -- upstream is
reused untouched. This build hardens it and adds a thorough test net.

- Blocking-node checkpointing. When the cache is on, the heavy multi-input
  ops -- join, multijoin, crossjoin, antijoin, union, reconcile (new
  _FLOW_CHECKPOINT_TYPES) -- are now always materialised as cache
  checkpoints rather than fused into a downstream query. A big join feeding
  a pivot/chart is now reused on every downstream edit instead of being
  re-executed. Single-consumer SQL nodes still fuse as before; pivots still
  always materialise (their columns are only known at run time).
- Fixed a latent multi-output port-collision bug (exposed by the above).
  The cache key was the node fingerprint alone, so a join's
  left_only / inner / right_only ports (and a filter's true / false) shared
  one __nbcache_* table -- the second port queried was handed the first
  port's data. The key now folds in the output port, so each port gets a
  distinct cache table.

Tests: +6 covering fingerprints (determinism, epoch/engine salting,
edit-scoping, sibling sharing, projection-awareness, cyclic omission), LRU
eviction dropping the backing table, incremental reuse with parity against
the cache-off path, invalidation on a write (epoch bump + clear),
count-cap eviction, and checkpoint reuse of a join across a downstream
edit. 5 structural temp-count tests that assert the per-pass fusion /
cleanup / dedup machinery now pin the cache off (their concern is the
cache-off path; cache lifecycle is covered by the new tests).
Suite: 231 passed / 0 failed / 12 skipped (backend 169, http 42, fe 20).

build 2026-06-20.142
  Pivot node: drag-to-reorder fields + Tableau-style indented sub-rows.

  Reorder fields by dragging. The Rows, Columns, and Measures sections are now
  ordered, draggable lists (grab the handle and drag up/down) instead of
  checkbox pools -- field order is what drives row nesting and column nesting,
  so being able to reorder matters. Each list has a remove (x) on every item and
  an "+ Add field" picker / "Add measure" button to append. Native drag-and-drop,
  no new dependency.

  Indented sub-rows (outline). A new "Indented sub-rows (outline)" toggle renders
  a multi-row-dimension pivot the way Tableau/Excel "compact" form does: a single
  "Row Labels" column where each parent value sits on its own row and its
  children are indented beneath it, for any number of depths. It reuses the
  ROLLUP/UNION machinery already built for subtotals (the prefix groupings ARE
  the parent rows), so:
    - Outline alone: parent rows are headers (blank measure cells), children
      carry the values, no grand total.
    - Outline + subtotals: parent header rows also carry their subtotal values,
      and a "Grand Total" row is kept; the Total column stays too.
  Ordering is parent-before-children (pre-order), grand total last; indentation
  uses non-breaking spaces so it survives the grid. With the toggle off the
  pivot keeps the flat, one-column-per-row-dimension layout (and full values,
  best for feeding downstream nodes).

  New config: cols/values field order is now meaningful; ``outline`` boolean.
  Old single-field pivot configs still work unchanged.

  Tests: 225 (backend 163, http 42, frontend 20). The pivot-node crosstab test
  now also asserts the outline layout -- one "Row Labels" column, a parent row
  shown above its indented children, blank headers + no grand total without
  subtotals, and a Total column + a "Grand Total" row with subtotals. A
  structural check confirms the reorder lists, the add pickers, and the outline
  toggle are wired.

  Sandbox note: no DuckDB here, so the ROLLUP path is verified by mirroring the
  proven SQLite-emulation output; the SQLite path runs end-to-end. No browser,

build 2026-06-20.141
  Fix: flatten progress now reports the reading stage on the ijson fast path.

  The flatten-export progress test failed on machines that have ijson installed
  (the fast streaming reader). The byte-counting wrapper only reports every
  ~256 KB, so a small JSON file finished the read phase without ever emitting a
  "reading" event -- the progress bar would jump straight to the writing stage.
  (The stdlib reader, used when ijson is absent, always emitted, which is why
  the sandbox didn't catch it.)

  stream_json_records now emits a final read-complete event after the ijson loop,
  so the read phase is always observed and the bar reaches the hand-off point
  before writing begins. No behaviour change for large files beyond the read bar
  now finishing cleanly at 100% of bytes; none for the stdlib path.

  Tests: 225 (backend 163, http 42, frontend 20). Added a regression test that
  drives the ijson branch with a fake ijson module (so it runs whether or not
  the C library is installed) and asserts a reading event is emitted that
  reaches the full file size. This test fails against the previous code.

build 2026-06-20.139
  Flatten JSON and Export now shows a progress bar next to the Flatten button.

  The export runs as a background job and the tab polls it, so a large file no
  longer leaves the button spinning with no feedback. The bar fills in two
  phases:

  - Reading (0-70%): driven by how many bytes of the input JSON have been
    streamed, with a live record count ("Reading JSON... 25,308 records").
  - Writing (70-100%): driven by how many of the relational tables have been
    written, naming the current CSV ("Writing CSVs... inventory_..._loans.csv").

  on an error the message surfaces inline.

  - flatten.py: stream_json_records(path, progress=) reports the read position
    best-effort -- a counting wrapper on the ijson fast path, and the buffer
    position on the stdlib array / concatenated-value paths.
  - session.flatten_json_to_csv_dir(..., progress=) emits {stage:"reading",
    bytes_done, bytes_total, records} while streaming, then {stage:"writing",
    tables_done, tables_total, detail} per table written. The synchronous
    entry point is unchanged.
  - server.py: POST /api/flatten/start launches the job (tracked in JOBS) and
    GET /api/flatten/progress/<job> returns progress + the result on done.
  - api.ts: flattenStart / flattenProgress; FlattenTab starts the job and polls
    every 250 ms, mapping the two phases onto a single 0-100% bar.

build 2026-06-20.137
  Optional encrypted password storage for SQL Server and REST API connections
  (Windows DPAPI).

  - A "Save password (encrypted)" checkbox now appears on both the SQL Server
    and REST API tabs (off by default). When ticked, the password is encrypted
    with Windows DPAPI (CryptProtectData) tied to your Windows login account and
    stored in ~/.json_csv_sql_explorer/secrets.json -- the same mechanism the
    keyring package uses on Windows, called directly via ctypes so we stay
    stdlib-only (no new dependencies).
  - The decrypted secret never leaves the backend: it is keyed by profile name
    (mssql:<name> / api:<name>) and filled in server-side at connect / fetch /
    load time when the password field is left blank, so a saved profile just
    works. The password is saved when you Save the profile (or, as a
    convenience, on a successful connect / load with the box ticked).
  - Deleting a profile removes its stored secret. Unticking and re-saving the
    profile clears it.
  - DPAPI is Windows-only. On any other platform, or if DPAPI can't be loaded,
    the checkbox is disabled ("Windows only") and a plaintext password is NEVER
    written to disk -- it falls back to re-entering each session. A new
    `secrets` capability flag in /api/features tells the UI which case applies.

  Implementation: new stdlib-only backend/samql_core/secretstore.py
  (DPAPI protect/unprotect + a base64 JSON SecretStore, with the cipher
  decoupled from the store for testability); /api/secrets/{available,set,
  delete,status} endpoints; a `secret_key` fallback in mssql_connect,
  api_fetch, and api_preview; a `savePassword` flag on both saved-profile
  shapes; and secretSet / secretDelete / secretStatus in the API client.

  Tests: 221 (backend 160, http 41, frontend 20). A backend test exercises the
  store with an injected reversible cipher (encrypted round-trip, survives a
  reload, delete) and asserts the no-DPAPI path stores nothing and writes no
  plaintext file; the profile harnesses assert savePassword defaults to false;
  a structural check confirms the checkbox + secret wiring across both tabs.

  Sandbox note: DPAPI's crypt32 calls can't run on this Linux sandbox, so the
  CryptProtectData / CryptUnprotectData path is written-to-spec and verified by
  the surrounding logic (availability gating, store persistence, no-plaintext
  guarantee) rather than a live encrypt; verify the actual encrypt/decrypt on
  Windows.

build 2026-06-20.134
  REST API load now honors the engine choice (it was silently always SQLite).

  The "Load into" selector on the REST API tab now actually routes the load,
  matching how JSON *files* already behave:

  - SQLite: the response is flattened into related relational tables (the
    existing JSON-flattening logic) -- a nested array becomes its own child
    table linked to the root.
  - DuckDB: the response is handed to DuckDB's native JSON reader, producing a

    used when loading a .json file with DuckDB selected.
  - Auto resolves to the session's preferred engine (DuckDB when installed),

build 2026-06-20.132
  Drag-and-drop file load. Drag one or more files from your file manager onto
  the window: an overlay confirms the drop, then a small prompt lists the files
  and asks how to load them (Auto / DuckDB / SQLite). Choosing Load sends them
  through the existing multipart upload endpoint (POST /api/load/files), which
  writes each to a temp file, imports it into the chosen engine, and cleans the
  temp up; the sidebar refreshes when it's done.

  Why a prompt rather than a silent load: browsers don't expose a dropped file's
  real filesystem path, so the path-based loader can't be used directly. The
  files are uploaded to the local backend over localhost (nothing leaves your
  machine) and the prompt is where you pick the destination engine.

build 2026-06-20.126
  Fixed: leaving the Node tab for the Journal/IDE and coming back re-opened an
  old workflow into a brand-new tab every time -- including workflows that had
  since been deleted from Saved Workflows.

  Cause: the views are mounted on demand, so switching away unmounts the Node
  canvas and switching back re-mounts it. The "open this workflow" request from
  the sidebar is a one-shot signal de-duplicated by a ref inside the component;
  that ref is lost on unmount, so on re-mount the still-present request (holding
  a snapshot of the old graph) was consumed again and opened into a fresh tab.
  Build .122 made this visible, since loads now open new tabs rather than
  replacing the current canvas.

  Fix: the canvas now clears the one-shot request as soon as it consumes it, so
  a later re-mount has nothing to replay. The Journal had the identical pattern
  (re-loading a stale notebook on return), so it got the same fix.

  Tests: 213 (backend 154, http 40, frontend 19). New check verifies both the
  Node and Journal load requests are cleared on consume and that App resets them.

  Sandbox note: no browser here, so the mount/unmount flow is verified
  structurally (the consume-then-clear wiring), not by switching tabs live.
----------------------------------------------------------------

build 2026-06-20.124
  Added optional react-icons support, with the current icons as the built-in
  fallback. Important: react-icons is NOT installed and NOT a dependency -- the
  build still ships with exactly three runtime deps (react, react-dom, echarts),
  and by default every icon renders exactly as before. This is the scaffolding +
  fallback, ready to switch on after react-icons clears security review.

  How it works:
  - New iconPack.tsx exposes packIcon(name). By default it returns null, so
    Icon.tsx renders its built-in SVGs (today's icons). A commented react-icons
    block in the same file is the single switch point.
  - Icon.tsx now resolves each icon through packIcon first, then falls back to
    its SVG. With the pack off, behaviour is identical to before.
  - Only names listed in the pack's MAP change when it is enabled; everything
    else keeps its built-in SVG.

  Node icons that WILL move to react-icons when enabled (the two weakest today):
    - Aggregate: Step (a media triangle) -> Sigma (the aggregate symbol)
    - Combine:   Swap arrows            -> git-merge (joining streams)
  Node icons that will NOT change: Input (Database), Transform (Filter),
  Create (Table), Output (Download), and every per-node-type icon (Summarize,
  Join, Sort, Filter, Pivot, ...).

  The two categories were given their own dedicated icon keys (Aggregate /
  Combine) rather than remapping the shared Step / Swap icons -- those are reused
  by the Summarize and Join nodes, Map/recode, Reconcile and the SQL "Statement"
  button, so scoping the change keeps the pack from disturbing them.

  To enable react-icons later: `npm i react-icons`, then swap the commented
  block in iconPack.tsx for the active fallback (one file). Add rows to its MAP
  to move more icons over.

  Tests: 213 (backend 154, http 40, frontend 19). New UI-wiring check verifies
  the pack/fallback wiring and that react-icons is NOT in package.json (so the
  three-dependency rule holds and the fallback is what ships).

  Sandbox note: no network here, so react-icons cannot be installed or rendered;
  the active, verified path is the built-in fallback. The react-icons path is
  provided as ready-to-enable code, not something exercised in this build.

build 2026-06-20.121
  Fixed: the canvas right-click "Nodes" cascade didn't open the second-level
  submenu. Hovering Nodes showed the category list (Input, Transform, ...), but
  hovering a category never revealed its node list.

  Cause was a CSS overflow interaction, not the hover logic. The flyout style
  set overflow-y:auto (so a long node list can scroll). Per the CSS spec, when
  one overflow axis is auto and the other is visible, the visible axis is forced
  to auto too -- so the category list ended up clipping on BOTH axes. The
  node-list submenu is positioned just outside that box (at left/right:100%), so
  it was rendered but clipped away to nothing.

  Now only the deepest level -- the node list itself -- carries the scroll, via a
  new nb2-cm-leaf modifier. The intermediate category list no longer clips, so
  the submenu nested inside it shows. The leaf has no nested flyout, so scrolling
  there is harmless.

  Tests: 213 (backend 154, http 40, frontend 19). The UI-wiring test now also
  asserts the scroll lives on the leaf flyout and the intermediate cascade level
  does not clip.

  Sandbox note: there is no browser here, so this is verified structurally
  (markup + CSS), not by rendering the menu.

build 2026-06-20.120
  Temp directories no longer accumulate across runs.

  Every temp artifact SamQL makes -- the DuckDB on-disk database and its spill
  directory, per-result row stores, Parquet result temporaries, export files,
  and JSON-flatten spill directories -- already lives under one per-process
  directory (<system-temp>/samql/<pid>/) and is removed promptly: row stores are
  deleted when a result is evicted or cleared, Parquet and export temporaries are
  unlinked right after they are written/sent, and the JSON spill directory is
  removed after each load. A clean shutdown deletes the whole instance directory,
  and startup sweeps directories left by earlier runs that were killed before
  they could clean up (their owning process is gone).

  The gap: that sweep ran only at startup, so a clean run never tidied orphans
  left by a previously-crashed run until the next launch. A graceful shutdown
  (Ctrl+C / SIGTERM / window close) now sweeps those stale directories too, so
  the temp area is tidied at both ends of every run. The sweep only removes
  directories whose owning process has exited -- a concurrently running instance
  is never touched.

  Tests: 213 (backend 154, http 40, frontend 19). New: the shutdown handler both
  removes this instance's temp directory and sweeps stale ones from prior runs.

  Sandbox note: deletion of an open file while it is still locked is a
  Windows-specific concern; the handles (SQLite + DuckDB) are closed before the
  directory is removed, but the real on-disk teardown can only be confirmed on
  Windows with DuckDB installed, neither of which runs here.

build 2026-06-20.119
  Ctrl+C now shuts down to a clean slate.

  A graceful shutdown -- Ctrl+C, SIGTERM, or closing the window -- now drops
  every table (both loaded tables and temp/working tables) AND clears the
  session restore manifest. The next launch comes up empty with nothing loaded,
  and the instance's temp directory (DuckDB file, SQLite spill files) is deleted
  as before.

  Previously a graceful shutdown kept the manifest so the next launch would
  re-load your tables. That now only happens after a hard crash: if the process
  is killed without running its shutdown (kill -9, power loss), the manifest
  survives and the next launch still rebuilds from it. So: clean exit = clean
  start; crash = recover.

  Tests: 212 (backend 154, http 39, frontend 19). New: graceful shutdown drops
  every tracked table and empties the restore manifest. The session-restore test
  was reframed to cover crash recovery (manifest survives only when shutdown did
  not run).

build 2026-06-20.102
  Downstream nodes now follow every change an upstream node makes to its
  columns -- fixing renamed/added columns not persisting into later nodes.

  The bug: a Select node's field list was seeded once and never reconciled, so
  if an upstream Select renamed a column (foo -> bar) or a Formula added one,
  the downstream Select kept its stale fields -- still referencing foo, never
  picking up bar. (The engine always chained correctly; this was the inspector
  losing track.)

  The fix: a Select's fields stay in sync with the columns actually flowing in:
    - a renamed or newly-added upstream column (e.g. a Formula's new column)
      shows up and is kept by default,
    - a column that no longer exists upstream drops out (no more "no such
      column" downstream),
    - the keep / rename / type you set on columns that survive is preserved.
  Column discovery already refreshed live for every node's inspector, so other
  nodes (Sort, Dedupe, Unique, Join, ...) already saw fresh upstream columns;
  Select was the one caching a list.

  Tests: 197 (backend 146, http 37, frontend 14). New: a Node-run unit test of
  the reconciliation logic (rename propagates, new column appears, removed
  column drops, settings preserved, order follows upstream) and a backend test
  that an upstream rename and a Formula column reach a downstream Select both in
  discovery and at run time.

build 2026-06-20.100
  Two query optimisations for big flows -- projection pushdown and shared-
  subgraph materialisation. Backend-only logic; no new dependencies.

  Projection pushdown (column pruning):
    - Source nodes (input / directory / append-from-folder) now read only the
      columns used downstream, so a wide table behind a Select isn't fully
      scanned and intermediate temp tables carry fewer columns.
    - A backward column-liveness pass walks the flow from the materialised
      target back to the sources. It is conservative: a Select drives pruning
      (as does a chain of Filter / Sort / Dedupe / Unique above one), while
      joins, formulas, aggregates and rename-columns are treated as "needs
      everything", so pruning only happens where it is provably safe.
    - Sound by construction: an unused output port (e.g. a Filter's unwired
      false branch) contributes nothing; a filter's referenced columns always
      survive even when dropped from the output; and the source intersects the
      wanted set against its real columns case-insensitively.
    - Applies to every run / preview / export path. Toggle off with the
      project_pushdown config flag if ever needed.

  Shared-subgraph materialisation:
    - Run all now exports its file-output nodes in one shared pass, so a
      subgraph feeding more than one output is computed once for the batch
      instead of once per output. Write / chart / dashboard terminals keep
      their per-terminal path; a shared-build failure falls back to exporting
      each node on its own so errors still localise.
    - New backend: _materialize_flows builds several targets sharing one temp
      cache; export_nodeflow_many + POST /api/nodeflow/export-many stream each
      output from its own temp (with same-name de-collision).

  Tests: 195 in the bundled suite (was 191) -- pushdown liveness + correctness
  + soundness, pushdown oddities (spaced / keyword / unicode / function-like
  names, case, string literals), shared-subgraph "computed once" + cycle
  detection, the export-many endpoint, and the run-all wiring.

  Also added tests/test_optimizations_dual_engine.py: a standalone SQLite +
  DuckDB harness (29 cases per engine) to run on a machine with DuckDB and
  confirm both engines agree, including the out-of-ordinary cases above.
  Verified live on SQLite here; DuckDB paths are written to spec and exercised
  by that harness on your side.

build 2026-06-20.99
  Single-instance launch and a clean UI shutdown. Still one [.]exe.

  Single instance:
  - Double-clicking SamQL while it's already running no longer starts a second
    server. The new launch probes the port, recognises a running SamQL (via the
    /api/health "app" marker), and surfaces the existing copy instead: it asks
    that instance to raise its window (new POST /api/focus), or -- if it's
    running in a browser -- opens a browser tab to it, then exits.
  - The check runs *before* the data-engine import, so a second double-click
    responds in about a second instead of paying the full startup cost.
  - This is keyed to the requested port (default 8765); a port taken by some
    other program still falls back to the next free port as before.

  Clean UI shutdown:
  - Stopping the server from the UI now also closes the native (pywebview)
    window -- _graceful_shutdown destroys the window after stopping the server,
    so "stop server" actually closes the app instead of leaving a dead window.
    In a browser there's no window to close (the tab is the browser's to keep).

  Notes / unverified in sandbox: window raise and window close go through
  pywebview, which isn't installed here, so both are written to spec and need a
  real Windows run to confirm (Windows can also restrict foreground stealing, so
  a raise may un-minimise + flash the taskbar rather than steal focus). The
  helpers degrade quietly with no window present.

  Tests: +4 HTTP (health app marker, /api/focus, window helpers degrade safely,
  a second launch attaches + exits). Full suite 191 passed / 12 skipped.

build 2026-06-20.98
  Node bypass toggle, DuckDB memory env override, streaming exports, and
  parallel Run all.

  Node bypass toggle:
  - Every node with both an input and an output now has a small toggle in its
    header -- TD green when the node is on, red when it's bypassed. A bypassed
    node passes its primary input straight through (and is dimmed + dashed on
    the canvas), so you can switch a step off without unwiring it. The backend
    honours config.disabled in node_output_sql.

  DuckDB memory limit (exposed):
  - The DuckDB memory cap is still auto-sized to the machine, but can now be
    pinned with the SAMQL_DUCKDB_MEMORY_GB environment variable (clamped to
    1..1024 GB). DuckDB spills to its temp dir past the cap.

  Streaming exports:
  - Output-node exports (CSV / TSV / JSON / XLSX) now stream the result to disk
    in 10k-row batches through a server-side cursor instead of materialising the
    whole result in memory. With the existing 200k-row spill, a large export
    only ever holds one batch at a time.

  Parallel Run all:
  - Run all now dispatches terminals through a small concurrency pool, and the
    running indicator is reference-counted so it stays correct while several
    runs are in flight. Flow temp tables are namespaced with a per-run token, so
    concurrent runs (parallel Run all, or two browser tabs) can no longer
    collide on temp-table names or drop each other's tables.
  - Honest note: the engines serialise the heavy materialisation themselves
    (DuckDB holds a connection lock and already multithreads within a query;
    SQLite locks on writes), so the wall-clock win is mostly overlapping file
    I/O and running terminals that sit on different engines. The bigger gain is
    the concurrency-safety fix from per-run temp names.

  Migration: none. Workflows load unchanged; bypass defaults to on.

  Tests: +4 backend (bypass passthrough, unique flow temp names, streaming
  export, DuckDB memory override) and frontend layout guards for the toggle
  and the parallel pool. Full suite 187 passed / 12 skipped.

build 2026-06-20.86
  Five more transform nodes.

  - Map / recode (Transform): remap a column's values via value->new-value rules
    (e.g. NY -> New York). Unmatched values pass through or fall back to a default.
  - Parse / cast (Transform): parse a text column into a number, integer, or date.
    Numbers strip a grouping separator (default comma) first; dates parse ISO-ish
    on SQLite, with a format string honoured on DuckDB (strptime).
  - Top N per group (Aggregate): keep the top N rows per group, ranked by a column
    (e.g. top 3 orders per customer); empty group = overall top N. Uses
    ROW_NUMBER() so it works on both engines.
  - Cross join (Combine): cartesian product of the left and right inputs -- every
    left row paired with every right row (e.g. calendar x store), no keys needed.
  - Coalesce columns (Transform): collapse several columns into the first non-null
    value (e.g. phone_home, phone_work -> phone); priority follows column order.

  All five are clean on both engines; only the Parse node's date format is DuckDB-
  specific (SQLite ignores it and parses ISO-ish), which the inspector calls out.

  Tests: backend tests for all five (incl. error paths); the UI wiring guard now
  covers them. Full suite 177 passed / 12 skipped. SQLite paths verified live;
  the DuckDB-specific Parse date-format path is unrun in the sandbox.

build 2026-06-20.85
  Performance + memory: deep-dive pass (closing out the optimization work).

  Implemented this build
  - On-canvas charts are now memoized (React.memo on ChartView + a stable
    fallback element). Previously every chart/dashboard pane re-ran ECharts on
    EVERY Nodebook render -- so dragging any node redrew every chart. Now a chart
    only redraws when its own data changes. This was the real per-render hot path
    and the biggest remaining win.
  - Initial chart hydration is staggered one chart per animation frame instead of
    firing every chart synchronously, so opening a flow with several charts / a
    full dashboard no longer blocks the main thread in one burst.

  Deep-dive audit (what's already optimal -- verified, not changed)
  - Backend: tables auto-index id/code/key columns (<=2M rows), results spill to
    parquet, loads stream in chunks, the result cache is byte-budgeted, and
    column probes are cached per compile. Joins/filters already hit indexes.
  - Frontend: wires render in a memoized layer, drag/marquee/pan are rAF-throttled,
    the data grid is row-virtualized, multi-input column fetches are batched, graph
    persistence is debounced, undo is bounded (80), and previews are capped (5000
    rows). refreshHist is O(1).

  Deliberately NOT done, with reasons (so this is genuinely "finished")
  - Per-node React.memo split: the deep-dive showed the dominant render cost was
    ECharts redraw (now fixed) + wires (already memoized); the remaining node-div
    reconciliation is cheap and rAF-throttled, so a 400-line untested extraction
    of the node render is a scale-only win not worth the risk of silently breaking
    the canvas. Parked for the Playwright browser-test harness (the next infra
    step) so it can be verified rather than shipped blind.
  - Intermediate-result caching across previews: low ROI -- previews almost always
    follow an edit (so the structural signature changes and the cache misses) -- and
    it would complicate the temp-table lifecycle. Not worth the risk.
  - Lighter graph signature: the rAF throttle already caps the sub-millisecond
    JSON.stringify; a manual revision counter would risk stale column lists.
  - Diff-based undo: history is already bounded at 80 snapshots.

  Tests: layout guards now assert the memoized ChartView, the stable fallback, and
  the staggered hydration. Full suite 172 passed / 12 skipped. The chart render
  win is browser-only, so please click-test: open a flow with a chart or dashboard
  and drag nodes around -- the charts should no longer flicker/redraw.

build 2026-06-20.84
  New nodes + canvas UX (batch 2 of 2).

  New nodes
  - Anti / semi join (Combine): keeps rows from the LEFT input based on matches
    in the RIGHT. Anti = left rows with no match; Semi = left rows that DO have a
    match (no row multiplication). Only the left columns pass through. (The plain
    Join node's left-only / right-only ports still cover anti-join too; this is a
    clearer, purpose-built node and adds the missing semi-join.)
  - Group concat (Aggregate): the inverse of Explode -- collapses rows into one
    delimited value per group, with optional DISTINCT and a custom separator.
    Empty group rolls the whole table into one value. (SQLite group_concat /
    DuckDB string_agg.)
  - Date / time (Transform): extract a part (year/quarter/month/week/day/day-of-
    year/weekday/hour/minute/second), truncate to year/month/day/hour, or take
    the difference from another column (or now) in days/hours/minutes/seconds.

    set together (drag a node outside the selection to move it alone).
  - Snap-to-grid: a "Snap" toggle in the toolbar; when on, nodes snap to a 16px
    grid while dragging and the canvas shows a dot grid.
  - Inline node errors: a node that fails its preview/run gets a red outline and
    an error tooltip; the badge clears when you edit the node or it runs clean.

  Tests: backend tests for anti/semi join, group-concat (incl. distinct), and the
  date ops; UI guards now assert the three nodes, multi-node drag, the snap
  toggle, and the inline error state. Full suite 172 passed / 12 skipped.

  - Turns one row into many -- one per element of an array or list in a column;

build 2026-06-20.81
  Performance + memory pass (audit-driven).

  Performance
  - Dragging a node no longer refetches its input columns over the network. The
    column-fetch effect now keys on a structural signature of the graph (node
    types, configs, wiring) instead of node positions, so moving nodes around
    is free; columns are re-read only when the upstream actually changes.
  - Pointer drag / marquee / pan updates are coalesced into one requestAnimation-
    Frame per frame instead of running on every pointer event, capping re-renders
    at the display refresh rate. The marquee's final selection is taken from the
    release point (authoritative), with a live preview while dragging.
  - Graph persistence to localStorage is debounced (~500ms), so a burst of edits
    no longer re-serializes the whole graph on every keystroke / frame.
  - Backend: column probes are memoized for the duration of a single compile, so
    a shared upstream subtree feeding several consumers is probed once, not once
    per consumer (both the column inspector and the flow materializer).

  Memory
  - The result cache now enforces a byte ceiling (128 MiB low-memory / 768 MiB
    normal) in addition to the row cap, so a few very wide results can't blow up
    memory while staying under the row count. Eviction is still oldest-first and
    never drops the newest result.

  Still solid and unchanged: DuckDB result spill to parquet, streaming table
  loads, fused single-consumer SQL, and temp cleanup.

  Deferred (noted for later, lower leverage now): memoizing the per-node render
  with React.memo (a larger refactor of the canvas component, best done with a
  browser test harness), and a batch columns endpoint (the drag-refetch fix above
  removes the per-frame N+1, leaving only a one-time probe on selection).

  Tests: added a backend test asserting byte-ceiling eviction; layout guards now
  assert the structural-signature fetch, the rAF throttle, and the debounced
  persistence. Full suite 164 passed / 12 skipped. The drag/render speedups are
  browser-only, so please click-test: drag nodes around a busy flow and confirm
  it stays smooth and the inspector dropdowns no longer flicker.

build 2026-06-20.75
  New Multi-join node: inner-join up to 5 inputs at once.

  In the "Combine" palette group. Has five input ports (in 1 ... in 5) and one
  output. You pick a base input, then add each other input as a join that links
  it to one already-joined input:
   - different inputs can join on different fields,
   - each join can use several key pairs at once (composite keys -- "multiple
     joins per input side"),
   - joins can fan out from the base (star) or chain off an input you already
     joined, so "join to" lets you choose which prior input each new one matches.
  All joins are INNER. Output columns are every column from the base plus the
  non-key columns of each joined input; a name that collides with one already
  present is prefixed with its input (e.g. in3_amount), and the duplicate
  right-side key columns are dropped (the matched key is kept once).

  How this was checked: tested live on SQLite -- a 3-input star join with a
  composite key on one input returns the matched row with merged columns and
  dropped duplicate keys; a chained join (in3 -> in2) matches against the prior
  input; an empty join list errors. Full suite 156 passed / 12 skipped. The
  inspector (base/"join to"/key dropdowns) renders only in a real browser, so
  please click-test wiring 3+ inputs and setting a couple of joins.

build 2026-06-20.74
  New Group node: a mini-pipeline you build inside one block.

  A Group is an empty container (in the "Combine" palette group). Drag nodes
  into it and they form a vertical pipeline:
   - the GROUP's input feeds the FIRST node in the list,
   - each node below uses the OUTPUT of the node above it,
   - the GROUP's output is the LAST node's result.
  Drag the steps to reorder them and the chain re-links automatically. Click a
  step to edit its config in the side panel (its column dropdowns and Preview
  reflect the data flowing into it at that point in the pipeline). Click the
  group itself for group-level settings (label, notes, preview the whole
  pipeline, clear steps). The × on a step removes it.

  Notes / limitations:
   - Steps are single-input transforms (filter, select, formula, sort, bin,
     dedupe, split, summarize, window, ...). Multi-input nodes (join, union)
     don't fit a single straight pipeline and aren't intended inside a group.
   - An empty group just passes its input straight through.

  How this was checked: the pipeline compiler is tested live on SQLite -- a group
  of filter -> bin -> sort chains correctly, an empty group is a passthrough, and
  the partial-pipeline columns/preview the panel uses are verified. Full suite
  155 passed / 12 skipped. The drag-to-add, drag-to-reorder and click-to-edit
  interactions run only in a real browser, so please click-test those:
   1. drop a couple of transforms into a group and wire data into it,
   2. reorder them and confirm the output changes,
   3. click a step and confirm its panel + Preview show the right columns.

build 2026-06-20.71
  Three new data-prep nodes: Bin, Rank, Fill nulls.

  - Bin (Transform group): turn a numeric column into labelled buckets. Give
    a list of "value <= X -> label" cut points plus an "everything else" label;
    the node adds a new category column. Cut points are applied low-to-high
    automatically and nulls stay null.
  - Rank (Aggregate group): number rows by a field (row number, rank with gaps,
    or dense rank), ascending or descending, optionally restarting per group
    (e.g. rank within each category). Optionally keep only the top N per group --
    a quick "top 3 per region".
  - Fill nulls (Transform group): replace nulls in chosen columns with a value,
    zero, empty text, or a statistic (average / minimum / maximum over the
    column). Other columns pass through untouched.

  All three are plain SQL transforms that work the same on DuckDB and SQLite,
  and they snap into a flow like any other single-input node (preview from the
  panel, wire onward, etc.).

  Tests: backend tests for each (bucketing, top-N-per-group, null-fill) run live;
  full suite 150 passed / 12 skipped.

build 2026-06-20.65
  Fix: TypeScript type error that failed the tsc check on a full build.

  The Nodebook's onToast prop was typed to accept any string (kind: string),
  but the app's toast handler only accepts "ok" | "error" | "warn". Under
  TypeScript's strict mode, passing the narrower handler into the wider prop is
  a contravariance error (App.tsx, where <Nodebook onToast={toast} /> is
  rendered), so a real `tsc --noEmit` reported a type error and the frontend
  type-check test failed. Every other component already typed onToast with the
  three-value union; the Nodebook was the lone outlier.

  - Narrowed the Nodebook's onToast prop to "ok" | "error" | "warn" to match the
    app's toast handler and the other components.
  - Changed the one run-all "cancelled" toast from a non-existent "info" kind to
    "warn" (the only call that used a kind outside the union).

  No behaviour change -- this is types only; all runtime tests already passed.
  Why it slipped through: the sandbox these builds are validated in has no React
  types installed, so JSX/prop types collapse to `any` there and a real tsc
  can't run; the bundle check (esbuild) strips types entirely. The fix was found
  by tracing the toast types across App and the components. Full suite still
  143 passed / 12 skipped here; the tsc check passes on a machine with
  node_modules installed.

build 2026-06-20.64
  Nodebook: node fusion -- fewer temp tables, the engine optimises across steps.

  A flow used to write one temp table per node: a chain of five nodes meant
  five CREATE TEMP TABLE passes, each fully materialised before the next read
  it. Fusion collapses a run of SQL-only, single-consumer nodes into one nested
  query, so the database planner optimises the whole run (pushing filters down,
  dropping unused columns) and far fewer temp tables are written. Results are
  identical -- only the number of intermediate temp tables changes.

  Boundaries (still materialised, as a shared temp table):
  - a pivot -- its columns are shaped at run time, and it reads its input twice;
  - a node whose output feeds more than one consumer -- computed once and
    shared, never re-inlined (so nothing is recomputed and a random/sample node
    stays consistent across its consumers);
  - a SQL node -- its {{in}} token may appear more than once, so its input is
    materialised rather than duplicated into the query;
  - multi-input nodes (join, union) end each fused run at their inputs;
  - the flow's target itself.

  Safety: if a fused query hits an execution error, the whole flow is rebuilt
  node-by-node automatically, so the failure is attributed to a single node and
  behaviour never regresses versus the old path. Fusion is on by default and can
  be turned off with the fuse_flows config flag.

  Measured (SQLite, in-sandbox): a 4-node linear chain went from 4 temp tables
  to 1; a diamond (one node feeding two branches) from 4 to 2, with the shared
  node materialised exactly once -- all with byte-identical results.

  Tests: fused vs node-by-node equivalence on a linear chain, a diamond, and a
  SQL node whose {{in}} appears twice, plus the temp-count drop (4->1 linear,
  shared-node-once on the diamond). Full suite: 143 passed / 12 skipped.
  (Measured live on SQLite; DuckDB isn't in the sandbox, though the same nested
  SQL runs there and the per-node fallback makes a composition surprise safe.)

build 2026-06-20.63
  Second audit pass -- REST-loader hardening; the rest held up.

  Re-audited the back end and the new Nodebook code (SQL / write nodes,
  undo/redo, minimap) for breakage, stalls, leaks, and perf. Findings:

  - REST (URL) loader is now restricted to http(s) and size-capped. It used
    urllib directly, which also accepts file:// and other schemes, so the
    "HTTP(S) endpoint" loader could be pointed at a local file or a non-web
    address; it now refuses anything but http:// / https://. It also read the
    whole response with no limit, so a huge or hostile endpoint could exhaust
    memory; the read is now capped (512 MB) with a clear "too large -- download
    it and load the file instead" message.

  Verified healthy (no change needed):
  - Undo/redo is sound -- node, position, and config edits are all immutable
    updates ({...n, config:{...}}), so history snapshots never share mutable
    state; history is bounded (80 steps) and the watcher coalesces a burst
    (drag / typing) into one step.
  - The minimap recompute is O(nodes) per render (cheap), its resize listener
    is cleaned up, and it only mounts while the Nodebook view is active.
  - The SQL node's column probe routes to the right engine (DuckDB vs SQLite)
    in both source and {{in}}-transform modes, via the table-name-based engine
    chooser; wrapping the user query as a subquery makes multi-statement or
    non-SELECT input fail safely.
  - Result paging (DiskBackedRows) is SQLite-backed with on-demand indexing and
    guarded by an RLock with check_same_thread=False, so concurrent paging from
    the threaded server is safe; the canvas drag listeners use stable ([]) deps.

  Tests: the REST loader refuses file:// / ftp:// / bare-path / gopher:// and
    lets an https URL past the scheme guard. Full suite: 142 passed / 12
    skipped.

build 2026-06-20.62
  Nodebook: SQL node, write-to-table node, run-all, undo/redo, and a minimap.

  - SQL node. A node where you write a SELECT directly. Two ways to use it:
    as a source (reference a loaded table by name, e.g. SELECT * FROM sales),
    or as a transform -- wire a node into it and read that node's output with
    the {{in}} token (e.g. SELECT category, COUNT(*) FROM {{in}} GROUP BY 1).
    Read-only (SELECT / WITH ... SELECT); it composes with every other node and
    the flow routes to whichever engine the referenced tables live in.
  - Write-to-table node. A sink that runs its upstream flow and stores the
    result as a real loaded table you can query and join. Name it; re-running
    overwrites that table. The name is reduced to a safe identifier and the
    result lands in the flow's engine (DuckDB or SQLite).
  - Run all. One button runs every Output (export) and Write-to-table node in
    the flow, in turn, with a per-node status and a summary at the end;
    Cancel stops the batch.
  - Undo / redo. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y (also Ctrl+Shift+Z) and toolbar buttons step
    through canvas history -- add/delete/move nodes, wiring, config edits. A
    burst of edits (a drag, or typing in a field) collapses into one step.
  - Minimap. A pinned overview in the corner of the canvas showing every node
    and the current viewport; click it to jump. Auto-hides on an empty canvas.
  Backend: nodeflow gained sql (token-substituted, read-only) and write
    (passthrough sink) node types; session.run_nodeflow_to_table materialises a
    flow into a permanent table (sanitised name, overwrite, temp-swept) and
    _flow_engine_target now also follows tables referenced by SQL nodes;
    endpoint /api/nodeflow/write. Frontend: SQL + write inspectors and node
    rendering, a run-all orchestrator, an undo/redo history (debounced,

build 2026-06-20.61
  Field data with inline / edge spaces and embedded quotes is preserved
  everywhere.

  Audited every ingest path for fields that contain spaces or quote characters.
  The file loaders were already correct -- the CSV reader is RFC-4180 (handles
  quoted fields, embedded commas, doubled "" quotes, multiline cells, and keeps
  inline and leading/trailing spaces), and the Excel / JSON loaders pass native
  cell values through untouched; all loaders insert values as bound parameters,
  so a quote in the data is never a SQL hazard. The manually-entered paths had
  a gap and are fixed:

  - Create-table node + grid no longer strip text. A pasted/typed cell like
    "  spaced  " was being trimmed to "spaced", silently altering the data (and
    differing from the CSV loader, which preserves it). Text cells are now kept
    exactly -- inline spaces, leading/trailing spaces, single quotes (O'Brien)
    and double quotes (say "hi") all survive a round-trip. Numeric-looking cells
    are still trimmed before they're parsed (" 42 " -> 42), and an all-blank
    cell is still treated as empty (NULL). This applies to both the
    "Create table in workspace" button and the node's downstream output.

  Tests: a round-trip over the CSV loader, the grid, and the create-table node
    asserting that inline/edge spaces and embedded single/double quotes come
    back byte-for-byte (and that spaced numerics still coerce). Full suite:
    138 passed / 12 skipped. (DuckDB / Vite / pyodbc don't run in the sandbox;
    the loaders and nodes were exercised live on SQLite + the stdlib CSV
    reader.)

build 2026-06-20.60
  Codebase audit -- three correctness/robustness fixes; no behaviour change for
  normal use.

  Audited the back end for functions that break others, stalls, memory leaks,
  performance traps, and latent bugs. The structure held up well -- bounded
  result cache with closed-on-evict temp files, per-PID temp dirs that are
  swept at startup (so even a crash can't leak them), debounced background
  cleanup, cycle guards on the Nodebook graph walks, a row-count-gated /
  column-selective auto-indexer, and SQL-Server cursors closed in finally with
  a single-pass catalog query. Three concrete issues were found and fixed:

  - Statement splitter ignored block comments. A ';' inside a /* ... */ comment
    would wrongly split one statement into several (it already handled ';'
    inside strings and -- line comments). Now block comments are skipped too.
  - A free-text table name could create an un-droppable table. The Nodebook
    create-table node names its table from the (free-text) label; a name with a
    double-quote produced a table that later code -- which refers to it as
    "<name>" -- couldn't drop or count. Create-table names are now reduced to a
    safe identifier (and a digit-leading name is prefixed).
  - drop_table didn't escape the identifier. As defence-in-depth (e.g. a
    quote-named table created by raw SQL), DROP TABLE / DROP VIEW now quote the
    name properly on both SQLite and DuckDB, so any table can be dropped without
    a SQL error. (For ordinary names the generated SQL is unchanged.)

  Flagged for review (not changed): on DuckDB, execute() holds the connection
  lock against a concurrent CHECKPOINT but execute_cursor() does not -- it uses
  an independent .cursor(), which is the intended thread-safe pattern, but the
  asymmetry is worth a deliberate check on a machine with DuckDB installed
  (it can't be exercised in this sandbox).

  Tests: the statement splitter (';' in string / line comment / block comment),
  create-table name sanitisation + that the result is droppable, and dropping a
  quote-named table without error. Full suite: 137 passed / 12 skipped.

build 2026-06-20.56
  Nodebook -- six new nodes (Sort, Sample, Unique, Unpivot, Window, Browse).

  - Sort -- order by any number of fields, each asc/desc.
  - Sample -- take the first N rows, or a random N rows.
  - Unique -- keep one row per distinct combination of chosen key fields (or
    drop fully-duplicate rows when no key is chosen).
  - Unpivot -- turn a set of value columns into rows (the inverse of Pivot):
    keep your id columns, melt the rest into a name column + a value column.
  - Window -- add running / ranking calculations: running sum / avg / min /
    max / count, row number, rank, dense rank, lag and lead -- each over an
    optional partition and order. A calc whose name matches an input column
    replaces it.
  - Browse -- profile the incoming data inline (types, nulls, distinct counts,
    min/max per column), reusing the table profiler; the data also passes
    through unchanged, so it doubles as an inspect-in-the-middle node.
  The five transforms compile straight to SQL through the same temp-table
  executor as every other node; Browse reuses profile_table over the
  materialised input (no registry hack needed -- the profiler takes a FROM
  source directly). All clean up their temp tables after running.
  Backend: nodeflow sort/sample/unique/unpivot/window cases, the _WINDOW_FUNCS
    map, a browse passthrough + NODE_PORTS entries; session.run_nodeflow_browse;
    /api/nodeflow/browse. Frontend: six palette items + inspectors, and a
    column-profile view in the preview drawer.
  Tests: a backend test exercises sort (desc), head + random sample, unique by
    key + full distinct, unpivot (3 cols -> 3 rows each), a window running-sum
    that accumulates [1,4,9,16] within a partition, and browse returning
    per-column stats -- all live, stdlib + SQLite, with a temp-table-cleanup
    assertion. Wiring check. Full suite: 123 passed / 12 skipped.
  The Nodebook node set is now: Input -> Select / Filter / Formula / Summarize
    / Sort / Sample / Unique / Unpivot / Window / Pivot / Join / Union / Chart
    / Browse / Reconcile -> Output.

build 2026-06-20.55
  Nodebook review pass -- performance + memory fixes (behaviour unchanged).

  - Inspector field-fetch was ~400x too slow. In .54 the columns endpoint
    materialised the whole upstream just to read column names, which fired on
    every node selection (1.2s on a 10-node chain over 150k rows). It now
    probes cheaply with a zero-row compile and only materialises when a pivot
    is upstream (whose columns are shaped at run time) -- back to a few ms for
    the common case, still correct downstream of a pivot.
  - Temp tables no longer accumulate. Each flow's intermediate temp tables are
    dropped once its result is captured (paging reads a cached result, never
    the temp tables), so previewing many nodes across a session no longer
    leaves dozens of temp tables behind. Applies to run / export / chart /
    reconcile.
  - Reconcile now shares one build pass across its two inputs.
  Reviewed with 24 out-of-the-ordinary scenarios (all pass): 20-deep chains,
    diamonds (shared upstream), cycle detection, 500-value pivots (capped at
    300 columns), hostile pivot values (quotes / unicode / a "; DROP TABLE"
    attempt -- escaped, base table survived), formula replace-all, weird column
    names, count-distinct over nulls, summarize on an empty table, bad join
    keys, mismatched-schema unions, malformed filters (graceful errors), empty
    inputs, reconcile registry cleanup after an error, and bogus casts.
  Backend: session._flow_has_pivot_upstream, _drop_flow_temps, a collect hook
    on _materialize_flow, and the cheap/ materialise split in nodeflow_columns.
  Tests: a new test asserts the cheap probe creates no temp tables, that
    run_nodeflow sweeps its temps, and that pivot-downstream columns are still
    correct. Full suite: 122 passed / 12 skipped.

build 2026-06-20.49
  Code signing: opt-in signtool step in the Windows build script.

  - build[.]ps1 now takes -CertThumbprint (cert in the Windows store) or
    -CertPath/-CertPassword (a .pfx) and signs dist\SamQL[.]exe with SHA-256,
    RFC-3161 timestamps it (-TimestampUrl, default DigiCert), and verifies the
    result. It locates signtool[.]exe from the installed Windows SDK. Signing is
    OFF by default -- a plain .\build[.]ps1 still produces an unsigned binary --
    and -NoSign forces unsigned even when a cert is configured. This matters
    for bank IT, which commonly blocks unsigned executables (SmartScreen /
    AppLocker).
  Docs: README "Code signing" subsection with usage + prerequisites.
  Tests: guard test asserting build[.]ps1 keeps the signing step (cert params,
    SHA-256 + timestamp, unsigned fallback, valid param() placement). Full
    suite: 116 passed / 12 skipped.
  Note: signtool / PowerShell can't run in the build sandbox, so the script
    edit and docs are unvalidated live -- only the script's shape is tested.

    locally-loaded table still uses the local engine; mixing a remote catalog
    table and a local table in one statement returns a clear error.
  - Catalog tables are per-connection and are cleared automatically on
    disconnect. The existing "run a query and import the result into a local
    table" path is unchanged and still available.
  Backend: mssql.list_columns (one INFORMATION_SCHEMA pass); session catalog
    registry + load_catalog/forget_catalog; run_query routes catalog refs to
    passthrough; tables_tree lists them as engine "remote". New
    POST /api/mssql/catalog. Frontend: LoadDataModal action, Sidebar remote
    rendering, api.mssqlCatalog, TableInfo.remote/qualified.
  Tests: backend catalog-routing test (pure logic, no pyodbc) + wiring check.

build 2026-06-20.37
  SQL Server login: saved profiles + alternate-account authentication.

  - Saved profiles in the SQL Server tab: a profile dropdown + name box with
    Save / Delete. A profile stores every connection setting (driver, server,
    port, auth method, username, encrypt/trust/MSF, timeouts, read-only) but
    NEVER the password -- you re-enter it on connect. Profiles persist on the

    tkinter app labelled 'runas /netonly'. Username takes DOMAIN\user form;
    requires pywin32 on the SamQL host. Fixed a real backend gap: the connect
    endpoint now builds and passes alt_creds (split_domain_user), so the
    method actually impersonates instead of silently falling back to the
    current session.
  - There is no separate 'SQL Server exe' to launch for this auth -- the
    connection is in-process over ODBC under impersonation. The thing that
    varies by machine is the ODBC driver, so the tab now auto-selects the
    newest installed 'ODBC Driver NN for SQL Server' (18>17>13>11) via
    best_odbc_driver, on both the backend and the UI default.

build 2026-06-20.33
  - Fixed two DuckDB tests that only execute where DuckDB is installed, so they
    surfaced on the Windows machine rather than in the sandbox:
      * "duckdb change column type" asserted the profiler would report
        'VARCHAR'. The profiler reports the DATA-inferred type (TEXT / NUMERIC /
        DATE), so a column retyped to VARCHAR correctly reads back as 'TEXT'
        (and the fact it is no longer 'NUMERIC' is the proof the retype took).
        The retype itself was already working; only the expected label was
        wrong. Corrected to 'TEXT', matching the SQLite sibling tests.
      * "DuckDB sorted + filtered paging" passed the symbolic operator '>'.
        Filter operators are word-based everywhere (gt / gte / lt / lte /
        equals / ne / ...); '>' matched no branch and fell through to "match
        everything", so the filter was a silent no-op. Corrected to 'gt'.
  - Hardened result filtering: symbolic operators (>, >=, <, <=, =, ==, !=, <>
    and the unicode >=/<=/<> forms) are now normalised to the canonical word
    ops before filtering, so an unrecognised operator can no longer silently
    turn a filter into a no-op. The frontend already sends word ops, so app
    behaviour is unchanged; this only makes the filter forgiving of symbols.
  - New non-gated test "filter ops accept symbolic and word forms" proves '>'
    and 'gt' (and '='/'!=') filter identically on an in-memory result.
  - 107 tests pass in the sandbox (12 skipped, incl. the gated DuckDB battery);
    on a machine with DuckDB the two corrected gated tests now pass as well.

build 2026-06-20.30
  - Ran the strange-data battery through the JSON flattener (runnable in the
    sandbox) and the DuckDB ingester (gated -- runs on the real machine).
  - FIX (JSON flattener silent data loss): distinct keys that sanitise to the
    same column name were silently overwriting each other, keeping only the
    last value. E.g. {"a b":1,"a_b":2,"a.b":3} collapsed to one column = 3, and
    a flat "a_b_c" key colliding with a nested "a"."b"."c" path dropped one
    side. The flattener now maps each original key PATH (tracked as a tuple, so
    a flat key and a nested path that serialise the same stay distinct) to a
    disambiguated column name, keeps every value, and reuses the mapping across
    records so ragged inputs stay column-aligned. It also reserves the auto _id
    / parent-FK names so a data key like "r id" can't clobber a foreign key.
    Clean JSON is unaffected.
  - Confirmed robust in the flattener (18 cases, no change needed): deep
    nesting (300 levels), arrays of objects/scalars/arrays, ragged + wide (300
    keys) records, big ints / NaN / Infinity, unicode/emoji/control-char keys,
    empty objects/arrays/nulls, top-level scalar/object/empty, heterogeneous
    and mixed-type arrays, numeric/blank keys.
  - DuckDB: still not installable here (no module, no network), so the strange
    cases are exercised by a new GATED test that loads weird columns + awkward
    values (dup/blank/quoted names, >64-bit int, Decimal, NaN, NULL) through the
    DuckDB streaming ingester, queries it, reconciles two DuckDB tables, and
    loads flattened weird JSON into DuckDB -- skipped where DuckDB is absent,
    full coverage where it's present. The DuckDB ingester's dedupe/escaping is
    shared code already proven by the SQLite weird-columns test.
  - 100 tests pass (9 skipped, incl. the gated DuckDB battery).

build 2026-06-20.25
  - SQL Server import is now DuckDB-first with SQLite as the fallback.
    Session.import_from_connection picks the engine by availability *before*
    draining the remote result: when DuckDB is present it streams into DuckDB
    (better for analytical querying); when DuckDB isn't installed -- or its
    typed ingest rejects a value mid-load -- it falls back to SQLite, which is
    dynamically typed and always available. The remote row store is re-iterable
    (a list or DiskBackedRows), so the fallback re-drains the full result
    cleanly. The chosen engine is reported back in the result.
  - New DuckDBManager.add_table_streaming: streams (columns, row-tuples) into a
    DuckDB table in batches (never materialising the whole pull), inferring
    column types from a sample via infer_affinities and mapping them to DuckDB
    types (INTEGER->BIGINT, REAL->DOUBLE, else VARCHAR). It is atomic -- if any
    batch fails to bind it drops the partial table and re-raises so the SQLite
    fallback starts clean. Mirrors the existing SQLite streaming ingester.
  - Load Data > SQL Server: when DuckDB is available the tab shows a "Target
    engine" selector (Auto = DuckDB with SQLite fallback, or SQLite); when it
    isn't, imports load into SQLite and the hint says so. The route + api.ts
    mssqlImport now carry the destination (default duckdb).
  - Sandbox note: duckdb isn't installed here, so the DuckDB ingest path is the
    on-Windows item; the SQLite fallback, engine selection, and the pure
    affinity->DuckDB type map are covered by tests. 96 tests pass.

build 2026-06-20.22
  - Audit fixes M1/M2/M3 + L1 (see SamQL_audit_2026-06-20.21.md):
    * M1 (leak): tables_tree() no longer advertises "__"-prefixed staging
      tables (reconcile __nb_*). They stay in table_columns so reconcile still
      resolves them, but they no longer leak into /api/tables -> so they vanish
      from the SQL-editor autocomplete and the reconcile source picker (which
      consume the raw tables list), not just the sidebar. The sidebar's own __
      filter is now belt-and-suspenders.
    * M2 (perf): dropped the redundant _invalidate_counts() from materialize()
      -- the new __nb_ table is never counted (M1) and existing counts are
      unchanged, so a reconcile run no longer needlessly clears the whole count
      cache via materialise (the next /api/tables avoids a full recount of the
      user's real tables on that account).
    * M3 (latent crash): DBManager/DuckDBManager.sync_catalog() now take the
      engine write_lock around their shared-connection access, so a concurrent
      /api/tables can't race a write (incl. materialise's CTAS) on the single
      connection. write_lock is an RLock, so re-entrant callers are safe.
    * L1 (hardening): runReconcile holds a synchronous in-flight Set guard, so a
      debounced auto-rerun can't start a second materialise/reconcile pass for a
      cell before reconRunning (state) propagates.
    Tests: tables_tree-hides-__ asserted at both the session and HTTP layer.
    91 pass. Deferred (product/larger): M4 large-source auto-rerun policy,
    M2 keyed count invalidation, L2 reconcile-drill result budget.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
build 2026-06-20.21
  - Reconcile cell: auto-rerun on change. A reconcile cell that has been run
    once now refreshes itself (debounced ~700ms) whenever its inputs change --
    an upstream source cell was re-run (its result changed), a real-table
    source was reloaded (row count changed), or its keys / compare / balance /
    source selection changed. The first run stays manual.
      * Trigger tracks *results*, not keystrokes: editing an upstream cell's
        SQL without re-running it does not refresh the reconcile (consistent
        with that cell's own grid only updating on run). To match this, a cell
        source is now materialised from its last-run SQL (ranCompiledSql).
      * reconInputSig() is the change-detection token (source resultId /
        table row_count + spec); reconRanSig is stamped on a successful run and
        compared by a debounced effect, which collapses a burst of edits into a
        single rerun and can't loop (after a run the signature matches).
  - Column-name mapping intentionally NOT added: because a reconcile source can
    be a SQL cell, columns are aligned in the SQL (SELECT x AS id), so the
    colmap_a/colmap_b machinery is unnecessary in the notebook. 91 tests pass.

    reconcile cell now lives in the notebook alongside SQL / note / chart /
    pivot cells (add it from the toolbar, the inter-cell + menu, or "Reconcile").
      * NotebookCell: a reconcile card with left/right source pickers (earlier
        run SQL cells + loaded tables), key/compare chip selectors and a balance
        dropdown drawn from the two sources' shared columns, a Run button, and
        the existing ReconReport rendered inline. Drilling or profiling a bucket
        opens the rows (DataGrid) / profile (Profiler) in a closable panel

      * Notebook orchestration: on Run it resolves each side -- a real table is

        co-located "__nb_<id>_l/_r" temp table (engine anchored by a real-table
        source, else sqlite; mismatched real engines are reported, not run) --
        then calls api.reconcile and renders the report. Drill/profile reuse the
        resolved spec. Temp tables are dropped on re-run and on cell delete.
      * Persistence + graph from .19 carry these cells (two dep edges) and the
        sidebar hides the "__"-prefixed staging tables. Reconcile internals
        untouched. 91 tests pass.

build 2026-06-20.19
  - Reconcile notebook cell -- FOUNDATION (step 1 of 2; cell UI + run flow
    land next). The reconcile engine compares *named tables* in a single
    engine and cannot take a subquery, so a reconcile cell must stage its two
    inputs as real tables. This build adds that machinery, fully tested:
      * Backend Session.materialize(name, sql, target): CREATE-OR-REPLACE a
        named table from a SELECT, registered in the catalog so reconcile (and
        /api/tables) can see it. Guards a bad identifier / a write statement /
        empty SQL. New POST /api/materialize route + api.materialize().
        Tested incl. a full materialise -> reconcile producing correct totals.
      * notebook.ts: "reconcile" cell type, NbReconSpec (keys/compare/balance),
        leftSource/rightSource/recon fields, sanitizeRecon, and persistence
        (slimCell + parseNotebookFile). Round-trip + sanitise covered by the
        node harness.
      * Notebook.tsx: reconcile cells add two dependency-graph edges (deduped;
        a real-table source adds none); sqlSig/persistSig carry the sources +
        spec so the graph recomputes and the doc autosaves on change.
      * Sidebar hides "__"-prefixed materialisation tables (and the count).
    The reconcile internals were not touched. 91 tests pass.

build 2026-06-20.18
  - IDE child memoisation (audit #2, implementation). Sidebar, DataGrid and
    Profiler are now React.memo'd with value-based comparators, so they no
    longer re-render on every editor keystroke (App re-renders per keystroke
    because typing updates the tab state). SqlEditor is intentionally NOT
    memoised — its value changes each keystroke.
      * Prerequisite handled first: setSql / insertText / loadSqlIntoEditor and
        the IDE doSort + the grid's onLoadMore / onColumnContextMenu callbacks
        were rewritten to read live state via the existing refs (activeIdRef,
        edTabsRef, activeResIdRef, resTabsRef) instead of closing over the
        active tab/result. This makes them stale-safe, so a skipped (memoised)
        child can keep an old callback without acting on the wrong tab/result.
      * Comparators: Sidebar compares tables/history/saved; DataGrid compares
        page/sortCol/descending/hasMore/loadingMore; Profiler shallow. Callback
        identity is ignored (the callbacks are now stale-safe).
    Confirm with the render instrument: set window.__SAMQL_RENDER_DEBUG__=true,
    type in the editor — only SqlEditor should tick now.

build 2026-06-20.17
  - Dev render-count instrument (audit #2, measurement step). A no-op
    useRenderCount hook (free unless window.__SAMQL_RENDER_DEBUG__ is set) is
    wired into Sidebar, SqlEditor, DataGrid and Profiler so re-renders can be
    profiled on real hardware: set the flag in the console, interact, and read
    window.__samqlRenders. Used to decide which children warrant memoisation.
    Finding: SqlEditor must re-render per keystroke (its value changes), so it
    is NOT a candidate; Sidebar/DataGrid are, but their App callbacks close
    over the active tab/result, so they must be stabilised (via refs) BEFORE
    memoising — otherwise a skipped render would fire stale closures (e.g.
    insert into the wrong editor tab). Memoisation will follow as its own step.

build 2026-06-20.16
  - IDE render isolation (audit follow-ups #1 + #3). Two timers used to re-render
    the entire IDE on a tick:
      * The running-query elapsed counter ran a 100ms interval on App-level
        state, re-rendering the whole IDE ~10x/sec during every query. It now
        lives in a self-contained RunTimer that owns its tick — App no longer
        re-renders for it.
      * File-load progress polled every 350ms on App-level state; the polling
        now lives inside the ProgressModal, which owns its progress state and
        calls back to App only on done/error. App stays still during loads.

build 2026-06-20.14
  - Notebook memory (audit fix D): bound the rows the front-end retains.
      * Collapsing a cell now frees its retained rows (keeping the column list
        and row count); expanding re-fetches the first page (or re-runs the
        cell if its result was evicted while collapsed). An all-cells-run
        notebook no longer holds every result's rows in memory at once.
      * A per-cell scroll-load cap (MAX_RETAINED_ROWS = 50,000) guards against
        runaway infinite-scroll. The grid already virtualises rendering, so
        this is purely a memory guard; sort/filter still run server-side over
        the full result.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
build 2026-06-20.13
  - Notebook result lifecycle (audit fix C): the notebook now manages the
    backend result cache instead of leaking it (the engine keeps at most
    MAX_CACHED_RESULTS=24, LRU-evicted).
      * Eager discard: re-running a cell discards its previous result, deleting
        a cell discards its result, and switching/closing a notebook discards
        that notebook's results (they aren't persisted across a switch anyway).
      * Self-heal: if a sort, scroll-to-load-more, or a chart/pivot cell's
        source hits "result expired" (evicted past the cap in a big notebook),
        the source cell is transparently re-run and the action retried, rather
        than erroring. ChartPanel/PivotPanel gained an onExpired signal for this.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
build 2026-06-20.12
  - Notebook performance (audit fixes A + B): typing in a large notebook is no
    longer O(n^2) per keystroke.
      * The dependency graph + compiled-SQL (for stale detection) now recompute
        only when the SQL *structure* changes, on a 200ms debounce — not on
        every keystroke and not on transient result updates. Staleness itself
        is now a cheap string compare. Autosave keys on the persisted content
        signature, so running a query no longer re-serialises the doc.
      * Cells are memoised (React.memo): editing one cell re-renders only that
        cell instead of the whole notebook.
    Measured per-keystroke critical path (50 cells): ~22.8ms -> ~0.005ms; the
    heavy recompute now happens once when you pause typing. (Audit items C
    result lifecycle and D retained-row bounds are next.)
